title: Gloria Steinem in Her Own Words: On Trump, Roe v. Wade, and the Birth of the Modern Women’s Rights Movement - Ms. Magazine
content: As we grieve the passing of Gloria Steinem, Ms.‘s co-founder and feminist visionary, we’re looking back at some of our favorite quotes from her 50+ years of speaking and activism across the U.S. and around the world. Steinem was sharp, funny and infinitely quotable, and many of her interviews from over the years combine deep feminist insight with some snappy one-liners. The two most famous quotes attributed to Steinem are probably, “A woman needs a man like a fish needs a bicycle” and, “If men could get pregnant, then abortion would be a sacrament.” However, while Steinem said and popularized both, she made it clear that neither quote originated with her: The first is attributed to Australian writer and activist Irina Dunn, and the second, according to Steinem, was originally said by her frequent speaking partner Florynce Kennedy. Still, Steinem had no end of wise, funny, inspiring sayings of her own that other feminists will keep quoting for years after her death. Below are some of our favorites. “A feminist is anyone who recognizes the equality and full humanity of women and men.” “We are the women our parents warned us against, and we are proud.” “Women may be the one group that grows more radical with age.” “Men should think twice before making widowhood woman’s only path to power.” “Many of us have raised our daughters more like our sons, but too few have raised our sons more like our daughters.” “Any woman who chooses to behave like a full human being should be warned that the armies of the status quo will treat her as something of a dirty joke; that’s their natural and first weapon. She will need sisterhood.” “People talk to me about white feminism, and I say, ‘Are you kidding me?’ If it’s white, it can’t be feminism. I mean, hello? It either includes all women or it’s not feminism. …There is just no such thing as defeating sexism without also being anti-racist, and no such thing as defeating racism without also being a feminist.” “If feminism means anything, it means taking responsibility for ourselves: for our own lives and actions. It is not ‘women as victims’ but women refusing to be victims.” “Women are always saying, ‘We can do anything that men can do,’ but men should be saying, ‘We can do anything that women can do.’” “If I had married when I was supposed to get married, I would have lost my name, my legal residence, my credit rating, many of my civil rights. That’s not true anymore. It’s possible to make an equal marriage.” “A liberated woman is one who has sex before marriage and a job after.” “We know sexism is not inevitable. It’s only about controlling reproduction and therefore controlling women. If we have reproductive freedom, that is the ability to decide for ourselves when and whether to have children and what happens to our bodies, it can be reversed.” “It’s obviously ridiculous to say somebody is ‘pro-abortion.’ Nobody wakes up in the morning and says, ‘I think I’ll have an abortion. It’s a pleasurable experience.’ The question is not pro-abortion or anti-abortion, the question is who makes the decision: a woman and her physician, or the government.” “Women have always taken power over our own bodies, and we will keep right on. An unjust court can’t stop abortion, but it guarantees civil disobedience and disrespect for the court.” “If women are supposed to be less rational and more emotional at the beginning of our menstrual cycle when the female hormone is at its lowest level, then why isn’t it logical to say that, in those few days, women behave the most like the way men behave all month long?”‬ “We live in a democracy that’s one of the few in the world that’s never had a female elected leader. That’s kind of ridiculous. I mean, we’re choosing from half the country’s talent” “Remember, the Constitution doesn’t begin with, ‘I, the president.’ It begins with, ‘We, the people.’ ” “When people were saying, ‘You’re all bra-burners and all that,’ we had to work very hard to be taken seriously. We were still having to prove that women were being discriminated against.” “The truth will set you free, but first it will piss you off!” “Revolutions that last don’t happen from the top down. They happen from the bottom up.” Ms. is wholly owned and published by the Feminist Majority Foundation Yes! I would like to receive new content and updates.

title: Louisiana et al. v. Food and Drug Administration: A case working its way through federal courts poses a dangerous threat to abortion access nationwide. - National Women's Law Center
content: The National Women’s Law Center fights for gender justice—in the courts, in public policy, and in our society. The National Women’s Law Center fights for gender justice—in the courts, in public policy, and in our society. The National Women’s Law Center fights for gender justice—in the courts, in public policy, and in our society. A significant case1 currently progressing through federal courts poses one of the most formidable threats to abortion access since the overturning of Roe v. Wade. In Louisiana et al. v. Food and Drug Administration, Louisiana seeks to impose its anti-abortion policies on states nationwide, and the outcome of this case may dictate whether individuals can access medication abortion free from medically unnecessary and ideologically motivated restrictions. This case represents yet another baseless effort to limit access to essential healthcare and will most harm those who are already pushed to the margins. Louisiana and one individual plaintiff brought this lawsuit to impose a national ban on obtaining the abortion medication, mifepristone, through the mail or at retail pharmacies.2 In other words, Louisiana wants to force every mifepristone patient in the country to travel to a health center just to be handed the pill, even when they have already been thoroughly evaluated and counseled through telehealth and there is no clinical reason for this visit. This lawsuit is a clear attempt by Louisiana to impose its anti-abortion policies on the entire nation. Mifepristone is one of two medications used in the most common abortion regimen in the U.S., accounting for 63% of all U.S. abortions.3 Because mifepristone has been proven repeatedly, for over twenty-five years, to be safe and effective, including when dispensed via mail or retail pharmacy, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in 2023 permanently eliminated a prior in-person dispensing requirement.4 This evidence-backed action was long overdue, and necessary to support patients’ dignity and right to make their own private medical decisions. It was also crucial to expanding access to abortion care at a time when access to such health care was, and continues to be, significantly threatened.5 In October 2025, Louisiana sued the FDA to overturn the FDA’s action. Among other things, Louisiana claims that the FDA’s action impedes their ability to enforce their own state ban on abortion. Louisiana made the extraordinary request that the court block mail and retail pharmacy access for mifepristone nationwide.6 In April 2026, a federal district court paused the case and rejected Louisiana’s request to reinstate the in-person dispensing requirement throughout the duration of the litigation.7 Louisiana quickly appealed to the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals—a court known for its hostility toward abortion access—and that court temporarily reinstated the in-person requirement.8 Louisiana got what it wanted: the Fifth Circuit decision immediately restricted access to mifepristone across the country, including in states that protect abortion access, causing significant disruption and chaos for both providers and patients.9 The two pharmaceutical companies that manufacture mifepristone—both of which had already intervened in the case—filed emergency petitions with the U.S. Supreme Court.10 Over the dissents of Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito, the Court ultimately blocked the Fifth Circuit ruling that banned mail and pharmacy distribution of mifepristone.11 This allows patients and providers to continue accessing the medication through mail and retail pharmacies as the case continues in the lower courts.12 Mifepristone has been a cornerstone of abortion access since approved by the FDA over two decades ago, with extensive research over the past 26 years reinforcing its safety and efficacy.13 More than 7.5 million people in the U.S. have used this medication for abortion and miscarriage management, with a proven 95–99% effectiveness rate for ending early pregnancy.14 As countless studies, peer-reviewed research, and efficacy rating based on outcomes have increased over time, the FDA has continued to eliminate prior unnecessary restrictions on mifepristone, such as the in-person dispensing requirement.15 Telehealth for medication abortion—including mail and pharmacy access—has been available since 202116 and accounted for one in four abortions in the U.S in 2024.17 Telehealth access to mifepristone involves providers working with patients virtually to assess, confirm, and date a pregnancy, prescribe and dispense the medication through the mail or for pickup at a local pharmacy, and provide follow-up counseling as needed. In the wake of the Court wrongfully overturning Roe v. Wade, access to mifepristone via mail and pharmacy has become crucial to getting people the care they need in the resulting reproductive health care crisis. A study from 2023 revealed that the average American lives 86 miles from an abortion provider making a required in-person visit logistically and financially challenging, and even impossible, for many, even in states where abortion is legal and protected.18 This is especially true for people in rural areas, low-income communities, communities of color, and survivors of intimate partner violence, who already face the steepest barriers to in-person care.19 What Louisiana is advocating—barring patients from obtaining mifepristone by mail and at pharmacies—would impose devastating and medically unjustified burdens on patients’ access to medication abortion.20 Taking away the ability to receive mifepristone in the mail or at the pharmacy would undermine access to abortion and miscarriage care—and patients’ health and autonomy—nationwide.21 It would restore secondary costs—such as travel, missing work, or securing childcare—that often delay or prevent people from getting abortion care.22 And it would compound the national crisis of a shortage of obstetrician-gynecologists and rising rates of pregnancy care deserts and maternal mortality and morbidity.23 The anti-abortion movement expected that the Supreme Court’s decision to overturn Roe v. Wade would effectively end abortions —but it has not, and that is largely due to medication abortion access. Consequently, anti-abortion lawmakers and organizations are now aggressively targeting mifepristone. Louisiana’s case is one of many that have been brought to target mifepristone. It follows another one brought by an anti-abortion organization that sought to overturn the FDA’s approval of mifepristone or severely restrict access to mifepristone by re-instating onerous dispensing requirements, based on junk science and baseless claims.24 That case, Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine v. FDA (2024), already went to the Supreme Court, where it was dismissed for lack of standing.25 Similarly, the Louisiana case is fundamentally flawed and should have been dismissed from the start.26 Missouri, Kansas, and Idaho intervened in the case before it was dismissed and are now continuing to press forward with the case, seeking to impose a range of unnecessary and burdensome restrictions, including the prior in-person dispensing restrictions, on mifepristone access.27 Additionally, Texas and Florida initiated a lawsuit in December 2025 challenging the FDA’s original approval of mifepristone from 2000, as well as subsequent approvals and regulations facilitating access to mifepristone.28 Contrary to standard practice, the federal government under the Trump administration has not defended the FDA’s actions in these cases. It did not weigh in during the Supreme Court or Fifth Circuit deliberations in Louisiana v. FDA. Instead, the Trump administration merely requested that the court delay its ruling on this case until the conclusion of a “review” of mifepristone being undertaken by the FDA. The review is politically motivated; it was demanded by anti-abortion organizations who want the Trump FDA to reverse its prior approval of mifepristone. The pressure from anti-abortion organizations on the Trump administration has been so relentless that it reportedly led to the former FDA commissioner, Marty Makary, resigning before being fired by President Trump in part for not doing enough to restrict access to mifepristone.29 The interim FDA commissioner, Kyle Diamantas, has gone so far as to reassure anti-abortion groups of his commitment to their agenda,30 and Trump’s current pick to lead the FDA, Dr. Heidi Overton, has a clear anti-abortion record, including criticizing the FDA’s decision to allow mifepristone to be dispensed by mail and retail pharmacy and repeating false information about the safety of mifepristone.31 During his confirmation hearing, the nation’s top law enforcement official, Attorney General Todd Blanche, expressed his agreement with restricting access to medication abortion and said that the decision to make abortion pills available via mail and pharmacy was “wrong.”32 He is now under pressure from anti-abortion policymakers to “resolve” the Louisiana v. FDA case and impose in-person dispensing for mifepristone nationwide.33 While this plays out in the courts and at the federal level, anti-abortion state legislators are also moving to restrict access to medication abortion. In 2025, 89 bills attacking medication abortion were introduced across 27 states.34 At the midpoint in the 2026 legislative sessions, 21 states have introduced 58 bills that would criminalize the sale, purchase, or distribution of medication abortion, and four of these have been enacted.35 These relentless assaults on access to safe and effective medication abortion are part of a coordinated attack on dignified access to necessary reproductive healthcare. title: What a start, Filipe Luís! Monaco fight back v PSG, top of Ligue 1 🎥 - Yahoo Sports
content: Filipe Luís achieved a major result right at the start of his stint in charge of Monaco. The principality side came from behind to beat PSG 2-1 at the Parc des Princes this Friday (4) and maintained its 100% record this season. title: This 4,300-Mile CT5-V Blackwing Already Had Its Engine Replaced — It Still Sold For $104K - Yahoo Autos
content: A 2025 Cadillac CT5-V Blackwing with only about 4,300 miles has packed an unusual amount of history into its short life. Despite already passing through two previous owners and receiving a replacement engine, someone still paid six figures to put it in their garage. Fair enough, the car has a desirable specification, combining Cadillac's 668-horsepower supercharged V8 with a six-speed manual, rear-wheel drive, carbon-ceramic brakes, and the track-focused Precision Package. According to Cars & Bids, the Drift Metallic Blackwing sold after the auction for $104,350 on August 31. The listing shows a clean Delaware title, no reported accidents or mileage discrepancies, and no notable modifications according to the selling dealer. The engine replacement naturally became a major topic in the auction's comment section. DelawareCadillac, the selling dealer, said it understood the original engine had been replaced because of an oil-pressure issue and provided additional context about what Cadillac installed in its place. Cadillac warranty replacements for Blackwing engines use complete new hand-built engines rather than repaired or partially rebuilt units. While the dealer described the cause as its understanding rather than presenting a detailed diagnosis, it specifically pointed to an oil-pressure issue. It's important to note that this isn't being described as an aftermarket engine swap or modification, but as a Cadillac warranty replacement involving another complete Blackwing engine. The Cars & Bids listing also shows subsequent maintenance, including an oil and filter change, transmission service, and tire rotation at 3,725 miles in April 2026. No accidents or mileage discrepancies appear on the attached Carfax report. Under the hood sits Cadillac's supercharged 6.2-liter LT4 V8, rated at 668 horsepower and 659 lb-ft of torque. A six-speed manual sends all of that power exclusively to the rear wheels. Its Precision Package adds stiffer springs, a larger front stabilizer bar, revised suspension bushings, recalibrated Magnetic Ride Control dampers, revised steering, and additional chassis tuning. Carbon-ceramic brakes are included as well. The original window sticker also lists equipment including a panoramic sunroof, two-tone Sky Cool Gray and Jet Black leather, heated and ventilated front seats, a head-up display, carbon-fiber interior trim, and an AKG premium audio system. Cars & Bids recorded 15 bids before the car ultimately sold after the auction for $104,350. That's roughly $25,000 below its reported original sticker price of $129,185, despite the Blackwing having accumulated only about 4,300 miles. Two previous owners and an engine replacement could understandably give a buyer plenty to investigate before spending six figures. The clean history report, warranty replacement, low mileage, and desirable specification provide important context, however, and the eventual buyer clearly decided the numbers still made sense. The result also shows how much appeal the CT5-V Blackwing still has among enthusiasts. A 668-hp, rear-wheel-drive luxury sedan with a hand-built supercharged V8 and six-speed manual is an increasingly unusual combination, and even this example's complicated early history couldn't keep it below six figures. title: Vernon V. Manley - West Central Tribune
content:
Vernon Manley, 82, of Willmar, died at 3:00 a.m. Thursday, September 3, 2026, at Bethesda Grand in Willmar, with family by his side. After several years of health struggles, Jesus Christ welcomed him into heaven. His funeral service will be at 1:30 p.m. Wednesday, September 9, at Willmar Bible Church. Visitation will be from 12:00 p.m. until the time of the service at the church. Burial will be at Fairview Cemetery in Willmar. Memorials are preferred to Bethesda Hospice. Arrangements are with Harvey Anderson & Johnson Funeral Homes. Vernon V. Manley was born December 6, 1943, in Willmar, Minnesota, to Vernon L. and Ella (Ruter) Manley. He graduated from Raymond High School in 1961. On March 24, 1962, Vern was united in marriage to Sharon Dahline at Tripolis Lutheran Church near Kandiyohi. Vern began his career in the automobile business in 1963, selling cars at YMC Motors in Granite Falls. In 1965, he and Sharon moved to Clara City, where he operated Vern’s Auto. In 1967, they moved to Faribault and later Grove City while Vern worked for AAA Insurance. Vern later joined Roth Chevrolet, where he worked for 10 years before opening a used car business with his business partner, Don Baker, in 1981. In 1983, they acquired the Ford, Lincoln and Mercury franchises. Over the years, the business continued to grow, adding Chevrolet, Cadillac, Pontiac, Buick, Jeep, Eagle, Nissan and Toyota franchises. Vern retired in 1997 after a 35-year career in the automobile business. Retirement gave Vern the opportunity to devote more of his time to what mattered most to him- his faith, bus driving, and his family. For the next 20 years, he especially enjoyed spending time with his six grandchildren and being part of their lives. Vern is survived by his wife, Sharon; their three children, Steven Manley, Lisa Bury, and Troy (Shanon) Manley; six grandchildren, Justin (Clara) Bury, Joshua (Mercedes) Bury, Zachary (Isabelle) Manley, Tyson Manley, Cooper Manley, and Aspen Manley; his sister, Connie Niemeyer; sister-in-law, Denise Manley; and several nieces and nephews. title: Ipswich Town v Liverpool: How the players rated - BBC
content: Isak's early double gives Liverpool victory over Ipswich Alexander Isak's two early goals set Liverpool on the way to their first Premier League win of the season - and a first for new manager Andoni Iraola - at Ipswich Town. Here's how I rated the players and you can see how you scored them below. Liverpool beat Ipswich Town at Portman Road on Friday night Kjell Scherpen: Desperately poor for Alexander Isak's early goal. Weak and meant Ipswich got off to the worst possible start. A couple of decent saves but the damage was done. 4 Dara O'Shea: Led from the front as always but Ipswich's defence struggled against the movement of Isak and the creation of Gakpo. He had a hard time. 5 Issa Diop: Towering figure always willing to indulge in the physical changes but this was a tough night after those two early Liverpool goals. 6 Jacob Greaves: Stern test against the inspired Cody Gakpo, showing the quality he will face in the Premier League. 5 Leif Davis: Tested defensively but was always competitive. Lent weight to attacks and had a chance with a far post header. 6 Sasa Lukic: Will bring experience to Ipswich Town but on this night Liverpool's midfield was too powerful. 5 Exequiel Palacios: Tried to bring some composure to Ipswich Town's game but was fighting a losing battle. 6 Abdul Fatawu: Pace but little end product. Energetic but erratic. 5 Julio Enciso: Ipswich's main threat. Tireless. Might have done more with the final ball but never gave up even when odds were against him. 7 Daizen Maeda: Anonymous. Made no impact at all and no surprise when taken off. 5 Emersonn: Battled hard but no luck against Van Dijk and Jacquet. 5 Jack Clarke (on 66 Maeda): Introduced when the game was lost. 5 Zian Flemming (on 66, Emersonn): Couple of bustling contributions. 5 Subs not used: Walton, Furlong, Kipre, Florentino, Nunez Alisson: Lucky to get away with misjudging a first-half corner. Important interventions by being in the right place at the right time. 7 Virgil van Dijk: Usual unruffled self in the face of some frantic Ipswich Town attacking. 7 Jeremy Jacquet: Solid alongside Van Dijk. Continues to look a very fine acquisition. 6 Milos Kerkez: Occasionally troubled by Fatawu's pace but never in huge difficulties. 6 Dominik Szoboszlai: Driving runs from midfield and always willing to test the keeper. Iraola should never use him at right-back. 7 Alexis Mac Allister: Still not quite at his best. Too many misplaced passes but never hides or shirks responsibility. 6 Florian Wirtz: Busy but occasionally lightweight. Finally showed why Liverpool bought him. 8 Victor Munoz: Willing and pacy out wide but could have delivered more end product. 6 Cody Gakpo: Could have been playing for Manchester City. Two superb passes for Isak's opening goals, Truly outstanding performance. 9 Bradley Barcola (on 64, Munoz): Showed one or two flashes of the lightning pace the £123m signing will bring to Liverpool. 5 Ryan Gravenberch (on 64, Isak): Brought on to shut down any potential Ipswich Town revival. title: Olympus Spa v. Armstrong (U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals, May 29, 2025) - Free Speech Center
content: Home » Articles » Case » Anti-Discrimination Laws » Olympus Spa v. Armstrong (U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals, May 29, 2025) The 9th Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that a spa owner in Olympus, Wash., violated the state's anti-discrimination laws by barring transgender women who had not undergone gender confirmation surgery from his all-nude spa open to women only. The owner claimed this was a violation of his First Amendment rights. (iStock illustration) One of the more fascinating cases that is being appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court is a case involving two Korean spas operated in Washington state by Myoon Woon Lee. He is appealing a judgment by Washington’s Human Rights Commission that he has violated the Washington Law Against Discrimination by attempting to exclude transgender individuals who have not yet received gender confirmation surgery affecting their genitalia from an all-nude spa that is only open to biological women or cis-gender males who have undergone such surgery. After a district court dismissed the complaint, the U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed in a decision rejecting arguments that the spas were exercising First Amendment rights of freedom of speech, the free exercise of religion, and freedom of association. The majority opinion was authored by Judge M. Margaret McKeown, a Clinton appointee who has been serving on the Court since 1998. The Court cited the law that prohibited discrimination based on “race, creed, color, national origin, citizenship or immigration status, sex,” including such discrimination that would bar the “full enjoyment of any of the accommodations, advantages, facilities, or privileges of any place of public resort, accommodation, assemblage, or amusement.” An amendment to the law prohibited discrimination based on “sexual orientation” explaining that it applied to “heterosexuality, homosexuality, bisexuality, and gender expression or identity.” It did permit “the maintenance of certain ‘gender-segregated facilities,’ such as ‘restrooms, locker rooms, dressing rooms,’ and similar spaces, so long as the facility does not remove or otherwise take action against a person for reasons ‘related to their gender expression or gender identity.’” Applying intermediate scrutiny, the court rejected the argument that the government had compelled speech by requiring the spa to affirm that it would provide equal access “for all customers ‘without regard to . . . sexual orientation or gender identity.’”  It believed the law regulated conduct rather than speech and that any “incidental restriction” on speech was “no greater than is essential to eliminate discriminatory conduct.” The spas’ owners argued that they had excluded biological men from the spa on the basis of their Christian faith that opposed “the mixing of nude persons of the opposite sex who are not married to one another.” Citing Employment Division, Department of Human Resources v. Smith (1990), the Court drew a sharp line between the protection of religious belief and action and required only a rational basis to neutral and generally applicable laws that only incidentally burdened religion. The Court distinguished this case from the decision in Masterpiece Cakeshop v. Colorado Civil Rights Commission (2018), where the Court had found hostility toward the religious beliefs of the business owner. In addressing the arguments from freedom of association, the Court denied that the spa was a place of “intimate association.” Recognizing legitimate “private concerns,” the court said that “nudity alone does not transform a public place or business into an intimate association.” Korean-born Judge Kenneth Kiul Lee, a Trump appointee, authored the dissent. He believed that the law that had been applied in this case “was enacted to safeguard women’s rights” and “does not cover transgender status.” He thought that the Commission should have been more accommodating to “members of a racial minority group who want to share their cultural heritage and provide a safe space for women and girls.” He further noted that the Commission had acted on the basis of a single complaint by an individual who had provided no evidence of ever having sought to visit the spa. He believed that the Court’s reading of the law “defied common sense statutory rules of construction, and the state’s own reading of the statue.” The judge also objected to what he thought had been an overzealous prosecution of an immigrant whose family had come to the US. In part to secure religious freedom and who was trying to provide service to the women and girls of the state. He cited laws that protected the privacy of females in shared bathrooms and other common areas” and the likelihood that a change in policy would result in the loss of clients. Claiming that the case was about “power,” he pointed to past discrimination against Asians in the state. As the dissent makes clear, if the U.S. Supreme Court takes this case, it could well base its decision on perceived animus against the Korean owners and their beliefs, on the privacy rights of customers, or on other grounds. If it were to address First Amendment issues, it might decide that the lower courts had drawn an unduly bright line between protections of religious belief and religious practice (the First Amendment specifically refers to free exercise of religion) that should be subjected to heightened scrutiny. It might also elevate First Amendment associational rights by putting greater emphasis on the fact that all customers were completely naked throughout the spa treatments. If this were a case involving federal law, or if such a federal law were involved, the Court might also question the lower courts’ interpretation of the relevant statues. John R. title: CPNRD Board approves V-TAPS to replace nitrogen management testing - centralnebraskatoday.com
content: (Central Platte Natural Resourses District, Courtesy) GRAND ISLAND – On Sept. 3, the Central Platte Natural Resources District (CPNRD) Board of Directors approved transitioning from the University of Nebraska–Lincoln’s current Nitrogen Management certification test to the V-TAPS educational program for producers in Phases II and III of the CPNRD Groundwater Quality Management Program. Instead of completing the current Nitrogen Management test every four years, producers will be required to attend an in-person V-TAPS program once every four years. The change is intended to provide producers with a more interactive educational experience focused on making nitrogen management decisions and evaluating how those decisions affect crop production, profitability and resource use. With up to 250 producers required to complete the four-year nitrogen management requirement each year, CPNRD will coordinate four to five V-TAPS dates and locations for those who are due to complete the requirement for the 2027 crop season. Following a public hearing, the CPNRD Board approved the property tax request and levy for fiscal year 2026/2027. The district’s total property valuation, as certified by the 11 county assessors within the CPNRD, is $26.28 billion, an increase of 6.82% from the previous year. The property tax request was set at $5,347,823.51, slightly below last year’s request of $5,347,828.91. With the increase in valuation and slightly lower tax request, the levy decreased from 0.021738 last year to 0.020350 for 2026/2027. The $23.26 total operating budget of $23.26 million was approved in July a 26.87% decrease from the 2025/2026 operating budget of $31.8 million. For a home valued at $200,000, the CPNRD portion of the property tax would be approximately $40.70. Property tax revenue supports CPNRD programs and projects including flood reduction, water quality and quantity management, soil health, conservation cost-share programs, forestry, land management, recreation and natural resources education. CPNRD serves all of Dawson County and portions of Buffalo, Custer, Frontier, Hall, Hamilton, Howard, Merrick, Nance, Platte and Polk counties. Darren Cudaback, Precision Conservation Specialist, reported on the Precision Conservation Management (PCM) Program, which includes 83 cooperators in the Gothenburg area covering 141,907 acres. The program has maintained a 100% cooperator retention rate. Cudaback shared the following results for irrigated fields: Because the number of acres represented varies among the practices, the results provide a comparison of participating PCM fields rather than a controlled, side-by-side evaluation. The Water Quality Committee discussed Nebraska’s ONE RED (Opportunity for Nebraska: Reducing Emissions and Decarbonization) Ag Data Bank and Grants Program and potential benefits for producers within the CPNRD. The Nebraska Department of Water, Energy and Environment (DWEE) is developing and funding the voluntary program, which will provide incentives to producers for participating in a secure agricultural data bank and for adopting practices and technologies that improve nitrogen and water management, soil health and overall farm efficiency. Producers who enroll in the Ag Data Bank will provide farm management information through an approved third-party service provider and receive an incentive for participating. Individual producer information will remain with the third-party provider, with data provided to DWEE only in an aggregated format by county. This approach allows producers to participate in the program and receive incentives without their individual farm information being provided directly to DWEE. DWEE will provide funding to Nebraska’s Natural Resources Districts to administer the program locally. The amount of funding that will be allocated to each NRD, had not yet been determined at the time of this release. DWEE plans to introduce additional program details at Husker Harvest Days, with enrollment in the Ag Data Bank expected to begin this fall and the Grants Program scheduled to launch in January.

title: Man City v Coventry: Key stats and talking points - Yahoo Sports
content: Life back in the Premier League after 25 years away does not get any easier for Coventry City. They visit Manchester City on Saturday (15:00 BST) in their third game of the new season. Manchester City flexed their muscles last time out with a 4-1 win over Crystal Palace. After only just edging past Bournemouth in their first game, new head coach Enzo Maresca has enjoyed an encouraging start in the unenviable position of replacing Pep Guardiola. For Coventry head coach Frank Lampard, things have been a lot less straightforward. They have lost both of their first two games and are yet to score a goal. The sense of a new era at Manchester City has been prevalent all summer and was rammed home even further on the final day of the transfer window. Enzo Fernandez arrived in a joint-British transfer record £125m deal from Chelsea, as did Iliman Ndiaye in an initial £60m switch from Everton. Given the way Saturday's hosts played last time out, both players may need to wait for their chance to start. Against Palace, it was Erling Haaland and Rayan Cherki who did the damage, with two goals apiece. Haaland has scored 19 goals in 20 Premier League appearances against newly promoted teams, which could be ominous for Coventry. As for Cherki, after his two assists against Bournemouth on the opening weekend, he scored the first double of his league career in the win at Palace. Only Bruno Fernandes, with three goals and one assist, can match the Frenchman's four goal contributions from the opening two games. Only Morgan Rogers, with nine, has created more chances than Cherki in the Premier League so far this season too, albeit the Chelsea man has been on the pitch for 63 more minutes. The arrival of Ndiaye means that, along with Cherki, Jeremy Doku and Antoine Semenyo, Maresca has four of the best dribblers in the division to call on. Although an opener at Arsenal was always going to be tough for Coventry, Lampard as disappointed by what he witnessed in the 1-0 defeat by Hull City on home soil last weekend. Given how free-scoring his team were in the second tier last season – 97 goals in 46 games – there would have been more hope of the side operating with a bit more attacking verve back in the top flight. But so far, only Aston Villa have struggled to make more of an impact in the final third than the Sky Blues in terms of xG, shots on target and touches in the opposition box. This fixture will not define Coventry's season, but Lampard will be looking for an improved performance from his team. The former Chelsea and Everton boss could also do with a boost given his own struggles at this level. Lampard has won just four of his past 32 Premier League matches (D8 L20), including just one of his past 19 in the competition (D4 L14), at Bournemouth in 2023 when he was in interim charge of Chelsea.

title: Brentford v Sunderland: Key stats and talking points - Yahoo Sports
content: Brentford are aiming to maintain their unbeaten start against a Sunderland side with one win and one defeat so far. BBC Sport takes a look at the key themes ahead of their clash at the Gtech Community Stadium on Saturday (15:00 BST). It's been a promising start to the season for the Bees, who have a win and a draw from their first two matches and were a bit unlucky to be pegged back by Leeds last weekend. None of Brentford's four league goals so far this season have come from Igor Thiago, who provided a division-high 40% of the Bees' top-flight goals last season, which helped earn him the squad's and supporters' player of the year awards. The Brazilian's total of 22 league goals in 2025-26 was second only to Erling Haaland and he had the best conversion rate of any player to have 25+ shots in the competition last season (26.2%). Thiago missed a penalty in the opener against Spurs and is yet to score in the league, with five of his seven shots so far off target. However, he scored in both of Brentford's pre-season friendlies and also found the net as a substitute in the Bees' EFL Cup win at Birmingham last month. Thiago enjoyed playing Sunderland last season, scoring three goals across the two league meetings. While Thiago started all but one of Brentford's 38 league games last season, 21 of Wilson Isidor's 32 appearances for Sunderland in last season's Premier League were from the bench, and the Haitian international has come on as a second-half substitute in both of the Black Cats' league games in this campaign. But lack of minutes does not mean lack of impact. Isidor has made a name for himself as a super-sub – his five Premier League goals from the bench since the start of last season is more than any other player in that time. Last weekend, he was at it again, coming on and scoring a late winner against Fulham to earn Sunderland their first points of the season. That was the second time he's scored a game-winning goal in the Premier League and came a year to the day since his only previous one - a 90th-minute goal that saw Sunderland beat Saturday's opponents Brentford 2-1 at the Stadium of Light. But recent history – and geography – isn't on Sunderland's side. Their last win at Brentford in any competition was in a third-tier meeting in August 1987 – since then they have drawn two and lost two. Meanwhile, they have won just eight points in their last 16 away Premier League matches in London, losing 12 of those games. They've lost their last three such fixtures, conceding three goals in each - one of those being the 3-0 loss at Brentford in January.

title: Nottingham Forest v Tottenham Hotspur: Key stats and talking points - Yahoo Sports
content: Roberto de Zerbi's Tottenham, who have lost both league games this season without scoring, now face a Nottingham Forest side who have beaten them in each of their last four encounters. BBC Sport takes a look at the key themes ahead of Saturday's meeting at the City Ground (15:00 BST). "It's the biggest problem, it's the biggest challenge and it's the biggest target to find the right mentality," De Zerbi said as he reflected on Spurs' defeat to Newcastle that left them bottom of the table. No points or goals from their two league games so far is not the start they envisaged after spending more than £300m on 10 new players this summer, but their beleaguered boss pointedly said: "You can't buy mentality in the transfer market." Despite their squad being refreshed by nearly a full team of new recruits, scars clearly remain at the club following their back-to-back 17th-place finishes and a dismal record of just 21 wins from 78 top-flight games (D16, L41) since the start of the 2024-25 season. Another telling statistic that points towards a lack of fight is that it's nearly two years since the last time they won a Premier League game from going 1-0 down. They've lost 28 and drawn eight after conceding first dating back to a 4-1 victory over Aston Villa in November 2024. De Zerbi's team selections have also raised eyebrows so far. Mitigation comes in the form of a few key players not yet being fully fit, but picking Pedro Porro as an advanced right winger, Conor Gallagher as a 10 against Brentford and chopping and changing his midfield is yet to pay dividends. They will now attempt to avoid losing their first three league games in a campaign for only the fifth time in their history and for only the second time without scoring since the start of the 1974-75 season. The Lilywhites will have to rectify their poor recent record against a Nottingham Forest side who are targeting a fifth league win in a row against the north Londoners for the very first time, having won both league meetings 3-0 last season. After they opened the season with successive defeats to Leeds, Forest steadied the ship with an impressive showing in a 2-2 draw with Liverpool at Anfield in which their xG of 2.3 comfortably outstripped that of the hosts' 1.61. To the fore in that game was Morgan Gibbs-White, with the former Spurs target scoring his 13th Premier League goal of 2026 - the highest figure of any top-flight player this year. While the Tricky Trees may not have secured all of their transfer targets, a significantly quieter summer than in recent years still brought in quality to the City Ground. Following the mega sale of Elliot Anderson, they actually turned in a profit despite spending nearly £120m themselves on the likes of club record signing Liam Delap, Sporting Lisbon defender Ousmane Diomande and one of the Premier League's best right-backs in Daniel Munoz. Head coach Oliver Glasner will be keen to get the club back to winning ways at home given they've managed just one victory in their last 12 top-flight games at the City Ground. Following their loss to Leeds on the opening weekend they will also be desperate to protect an impressive record of having not lost their first two home games of a top-flight campaign since 1924-25. One of the tactical tweaks that's starting to emerge as Glasner moulds his team is them becoming more direct with their passing. Despite a small sample size of two matches, 20.9% of their passes have gone long which is up from last season's average of just 12.5%.

title: Newcastle v Bournemouth: Key stats and talking points - Yahoo Sports
content: BBC Sport examines some of the key themes before Saturday's match (12:30 BST), with Newcastle seeking back-to-back league wins and Bournemouth boss Marco Rose awaiting his first victory. Matthias Jaissle earned his first top-flight win as Newcastle boss against Tottenham last weekend and could easily already have two victories under his belt, with only an injury-time equaliser from Liverpool's Dominik Szoboszlai denying the Magpies on the opening weekend. Nonetheless, his tally of four points from his first two top-flight games represents the best start by a Newcastle manager for 19 years and beating Bournemouth would take his team top of the embryonic league table - for a few hours at least. At Thursday's pre-match news conference, Jaissle was keen to stress that his side have one of the youngest squads in the Premier League and insisted the club are "realistic" about what can be achieved while in a "transition phase". If they are to maintain their early momentum, the Magpies will have to improve their surprisingly poor recent record in this fixture. They have failed to win any of their past eight league matches against Bournemouth and have lost the past two such meetings at St James' Park. Excluding cup competitions, their most recent victory against the Cherries came on Tyneside in July 2020, when the Cherries were managed by Eddie Howe. Like Newcastle, Bournemouth conceded an injury-time equaliser against Merseyside opposition in their first home game of the season. James Tarkowski's late strike for Everton denied Rose a first win last weekend, with the German bemoaning "slapstick" defending from a corner. Rose's side also led until the 84th minute in his opening game against Manchester City but eventually lost 2-1, meaning they have already dropped five points from winning positions. Failing to hold on to leads has been a recurring theme for the Cherries. They have surrendered 27 points after going in front since the start of last season - a tally exceeded only by Newcastle. That tendency to let victories slip away also helps explain why, despite losing just once since early January, Bournemouth remain the Premier League's draw specialists. They have drawn 19 top-flight fixtures since the start of last season, at least four more than any other club.

title: SpaceX’s Starship V3 produces more thrust than Saturn V and SLS Block 1 combined and is ultimately intended to fly multiple times per day. Yet after 13 tests it had still never entered orbit. Flight 14, tentatively targeted for mid-September, could finally change t - ScienceBlog.com
content:
Starship V3 leads on raw thrust, but Flight 14 may be the first test to convert that power into a sustained orbit. Rapid reuse remains a much more distant milestone. By The Long View
·
Edited by												Lachlan Brown SpaceX’s Starship V3 is powerful enough to make two famous Moon rockets look almost modest. The company lists 18.1 million pounds-force of thrust for its Super Heavy booster. NASA gives Saturn V 7.6 million pounds and SLS Block 1 8.8 million. Add those historical figures and the result is 16.4 million, still about 1.7 million pounds below Starship. Yet power at the launch pad is not the same achievement as orbit. Through 13 integrated tests, Starship upper stages had flown through space, approached orbital speed, deployed test payloads and returned through the atmosphere. None had been placed into a sustained Earth orbit. That contrast is not an embarrassment hidden inside an impressive statistic. It is a useful way to understand what launch vehicles actually have to do. Producing force is one problem. Converting that force into a controlled, repeatable transportation service is a much longer chain. SpaceX’s current Starship specification gives the V3 Super Heavy booster 8,240 metric tons-force, or 18.1 million pounds-force, from 33 methane-burning Raptor engines. The 72-metre booster supplies the force that lifts the complete stack from the pad. NASA’s published history gives the Saturn V 7.6 million pounds of thrust at liftoff. Its current Space Launch System overview gives SLS Block 1 a maximum of 8.8 million pounds during launch and ascent. The addition is straightforward: 7.6 million plus 8.8 million equals 16.4 million pounds-force. Starship’s published 18.1 million exceeds that sum by 1.7 million, or a little over 10%. On this particular measure, Starship V3 is more powerful than Saturn V and the first SLS configuration combined. The comparison still needs labels. These are published vehicle-level thrust figures associated with liftoff or early ascent, not a claim that all three rockets deliver their maximum at precisely the same millisecond or under identical atmospheric conditions. They also say nothing by themselves about payload, efficiency, reliability or destination. Thrust is force. It must first overcome the vehicle’s weight, then accelerate a rapidly changing mass as propellant is consumed. A launch system also has to survive vibration and aerodynamic pressure, steer accurately, separate stages, keep engines supplied with propellant and finish its burn at the correct speed and direction. A smaller rocket can reach orbit while a larger one fails because orbital flight is not a weightlifting contest. It is the successful completion of a timed sequence in which guidance, structures, propulsion, software and ground systems all remain inside their operating limits. Payload performance is another distinct measure. Saturn V was designed to send Apollo hardware toward the Moon in a largely expendable architecture. SLS Block 1 launches Orion beyond low Earth orbit. Starship is being designed around a reusable upper stage, high payload mass and later refuelling in space. Comparing thrust tells us how hard each system pushes near launch, not which complete architecture is better at every mission. That is why Starship can already hold the thrust record while still pursuing an orbital milestone achieved by far smaller launch vehicles. Several Starship flights crossed the conventional 100-kilometre boundary of space. Their upper stages accelerated to enormous speed and travelled between continents. Saying that Starship had never entered orbit after Flight 13 does not mean it had never reached space. Orbit is mostly about sideways velocity. A spacecraft can climb hundreds of kilometres and still come directly back if it lacks enough horizontal speed. In a stable low Earth orbit, the spacecraft is continually falling toward Earth, but the planet’s curved surface falls away beneath it at the same rate. For a launch from Texas heading east, orbital speed is roughly 7.8 kilometres per second before smaller corrections for altitude and Earth’s rotation. Just as important, the trajectory’s low point, or perigee, must remain above the dense atmosphere. Earlier integrated Starship flights used deliberately suborbital trajectories whose low points intersected Earth, ensuring that the ships would re-enter over remote water even if they could not command a disposal burn. Those profiles reduced the risk of leaving an uncontrolled prototype in orbit. They also let SpaceX test ascent, coasting, engine relights, atmospheric entry and splashdown without making orbital insertion itself an objective. Starship’s thirteenth integrated test lifted off from Starbase on 24 July 2026. According to SpaceX’s Flight 13 mission record, the V3 upper stage completed its ascent burn on all six Raptor engines, deployed 20 next-generation Starlink V3 satellites and established communications with each one. The satellites were test payloads on the same deliberately short-lived trajectory as the ship. They were expected to enter the atmosphere about 20 minutes after deployment. The upper stage also restarted one Raptor in space, an important demonstration for later orbital manoeuvres. Ship 40 then survived atmospheric entry, used its flaps to guide itself, flipped upright and completed a controlled Indian Ocean splashdown about 65 minutes after launch. It remained intact and afloat, giving engineers an unusually complete piece of returned hardware to examine. The booster result was less complete. Super Heavy performed the high-thrust part of its boostback, but only some of the commanded engines relit for the landing sequence and it struck the Gulf hard. Flight 13 therefore combined the programme’s most complete upper-stage performance with another reminder that the reusable system has two vehicles to recover. In capability, the flight approached many requirements of an orbital mission. In trajectory, it remained suborbital. The next test is expected to use Ship 41 and Booster 21. SpaceX reported a full-duration, 33-engine static fire of the booster on 28 August, following upper-stage engine tests. Static fires do not guarantee flight readiness, but they are major checks of the vehicles, engines, plumbing, pad and countdown systems. Current reporting places Flight 14 tentatively in mid-September. Space.com reported that SpaceX was believed to be targeting that period, while public regulatory filings have pointed toward an orbital profile and deployment of operational Starlink V3 satellites. The wording matters. SpaceX had not posted a firm launch date or Flight 14 mission page when this article was prepared. Mid-September is therefore a tentative target, not a booked appointment. Hardware findings, regulatory approval, weather and range coordination can all move it. If the expected profile holds, the upper stage would perform orbital insertion rather than follow another immediately disposable arc. Deploying operational satellites would also change the purpose of the flight. Flight 13 proved the dispenser could release test articles; Flight 14 could begin using Starship as an actual orbital delivery vehicle. Success would remove a conspicuous qualification from the programme’s record. After years of flights commonly described as orbital tests, Starship would finally have entered orbit. Orbit is not SpaceX’s finish line. The company describes Starship as fully and rapidly reusable, with both stages returning to the launch site and being prepared for another flight. Its June 2026 prospectus connects tower catches and rapid refurbishment with an eventual cadence that includes launching multiple times per day. That is a design ambition, not a demonstrated operating rate. A Starship upper stage has not yet been caught by a tower, refurbished after orbital flight or flown a second time. Super Heavy boosters have been caught, and one has flown again, but a repeatedly reusable transport needs both stages to complete the cycle. Fast turnaround also depends on much more than landing. Heat-shield tiles must survive with little repair. Engines and tanks need rapid inspection. The launch pad has to withstand repeated exhaust and acoustic loads. Methane and liquid oxygen must be produced or delivered, chilled and loaded on a large scale. Airspace, sea zones and neighbouring launch operations must be coordinated. Multiple flights in one day would eventually require these processes to become routine rather than heroic. It would require not merely a successful rocket, but an industrial and regulatory system operating around it. An orbital Flight 14 would be an unmistakable advance. It would show that V3 can complete ascent, insert its upper stage into orbit and begin delivering useful payloads. It would give SpaceX longer-duration data on propulsion, power, communications and thermal control in the environment where Starship is meant to work. It would not demonstrate upper-stage recovery, rapid refurbishment, repeated daily flight or large-scale propellant transfer between ships. Those capabilities are central to plans for the Moon and Mars. A vehicle that reaches orbit but cannot yet be economically recovered is a powerful launch system, not yet the fully reusable transport SpaceX advertises. ScienceBlog’s earlier examination of SpaceX’s shifting Mars deadlines reached a related conclusion. The hardware has made genuine progress, while the calendar has often described an exceptionally favourable path through work that had not yet been completed. Flight 14 should be judged the same way. If it enters orbit, the achievement will be real. If it deploys operational satellites, that will be another real step. Neither result needs to be inflated into proof that airline-like operation is close. Starship’s thrust record answers how forcefully it can leave the pad. Orbit answers whether it can finish ascent on a sustainable trajectory. Reuse will answer whether the same hardware can return and fly again. Cadence will answer whether that sequence can become ordinary. After 13 tests, the first answer was emphatic and the second remained open. Flight 14 may finally separate them. title: King Felipe VI, Queen Letizia and Queen Sofía Head to Oslo for King Harald V's Funeral - HOLA
content: King Felipe VI, Queen Letizia and Queen Sofía stood alongside Norway's royal family as the country lays King Harald V to rest. It's a trip that put three generations of the Spanish Crown in the same room on a day defined by grief and transition. Harald died on August 28 at the age of 89, closing a 35-year reign that made him Europe's longest-reigning monarch. The throne passed automatically to his son, King Haakon VIII, who swore his constitutional oath before Norway's parliament on September 1. Barely two weeks after his father's death, the new king faced one of the heaviest days of this transition: burying his father while stepping fully into the role himself. Spain's delegation was headed by Felipe and Letizia, with Queen Sofía traveling alongside them. Her presence carries its own weight — a reminder of the generation of European sovereigns who shared the stage with Harald for decades, and of just how tightly interwoven Europe's royal houses have become. Royal watchers are already drawing comparisons to other major farewells that brought the Spanish royals and Sofía together on foreign soil, among them the funeral of Britain's Queen Elizabeth II in London. Harald's funeral was one of the biggest fixtures on the European royal calendar this year, with the guest list reading like a continental summit: Denmark's King Frederik X and Queen Mary, the Netherlands' King Willem-Alexander and Queen Máxima, and Belgium's King Philippe and Queen Mathilde. Sweden sent a particularly large contingent, with King Carl Gustaf, Queen Silvia, Crown Princess Victoria, Prince Daniel, Prince Carl Philip, Princess Sofia and more. Japan's Emperor Naruhito, who attended the funeral of Harald's father, King Olav V, back in 1991, was represented by Crown Prince Fumihito and Crown Princess Kiko. Monaco's Prince Albert is also expected. The day gave Felipe VI his first face-to-face moment with Haakon VIII since the new king's accession. The two men have maintained a close friendship over the years, with Spain's royal household having already sent its condolences. The service was hosted at Oslo Cathedral. Harald's coffin was carried from the Royal Palace in a ceremonial procession along Karl Johans gate, turning onto Kirkegata en route to the cathedral, escorted by members of the royal family and representatives of Norway's institutions. After the cathedral service, a second, smaller procession carried the coffin to Akershus Fortress, where a private ceremony followed. Harald was buried in the crypt of the royal mausoleum, alongside other members of his family — including his parents, King Olav V and Princess Märtha, and his grandparents, Haakon VII and Maud. Afterward, in one of the day's most emotional moments, Haakon VIII and his family stepped out onto the balcony of the Royal Palace to greet the citizens who had spent the past two weeks mourning Harald, a king who led them for more than three decades. © ¡HOLA! title: Sutton's predictions: Newcastle v Bournemouth - Yahoo Sports
content: Newcastle have started the season superbly with four points, and it feels like they have changed the mood at St James' Park after a difficult summer. There's no doom and gloom about the place despite them losing several key players and, after predicting they would lose their first two games, I feel differently about their prospects now. But, so far, I've been really impressed by Anthony Elanga, and Yoane Wissa looks like he has got his confidence back. I like the way new manager Matthias Jaissle has set them up to hit teams on the counter-attack, and Nico Gonzalez looks like a sensible signing too. I called Newcastle "a development club" before their first game, because of the type of players they have bought and sold this summer, but while their midfield is quite youthful, they have now got Nico in there to give them a bit of extra clout. Bournemouth haven't won yet, but only because they have let leads slip away late on, first against Manchester City and then at home to Everton. Cherries boss Marco Rose is another manager who likes to play on the front foot and they are certainly capable of getting something here, even though I have gone for a home win.

title: Album Review: Sněť – V bažinách vědomí - therazorsedge.rocks
content: I first encountered Snet when they were playing in a support slot in a death metal show in Nottingham and was pretty much a fan straight off that, so you can imagine how excited I was to see a new album out and available for me to review! Snet play dark, dingy, rough death metal, in fact the album title translates to ‘In the swamps of consciousness’ which is a pretty good description of the band to be honest. Sludgy, fetid yet with good songwriting and atmosphere. Coming from Czechia and with song titles in their native language this could be a confusing release for many fans not conversant in that language, rest assured though, the language of death metal is universal and this album will sit right at home with the classics in your collection. Obvious comparisons can be made to classic Entombed material but Snet are not just another HM-2 clone band, yes, they retain some of that punkiness that made Entombed so great but they also feel darker and more evil, with some riffs almost veering into black metal territory. Standout track goes to  ‘Apokalyptický smaragd budoucí doby’ with its amazing middle section and breakdown, what an incredible riff! This album remains engaging throughout, absolutely reeks with atmosphere and is eminently headbangable, what more could you want from a death metal release? title: New Music | Friday Roll Out: V Torres, Mykki Blanco, Melissa Auf Der Maur, Black Bananas, EXP - Ghettoblaster Magazine
content: MELISSA AUF DER MAUR – BASS WOMB ROOM: My ’90s 4-Track Demos x Field Recordings Maybe it’s just me, but I’ve grown past the experimental phase some artists may have with releasing material that probably shouldn’t have been released, remaining decades old. Melissa Auf der Maur (Hole, Smashing Pumpkins) though, has decided to release Bass Womb Room: My ‘90s 4-Track Demos x Field Recordings. Cool. There are some songs here- vocals, guitar, etc. – but lo-fi indie tracks back in the 90s were better left for artists like Guided By Voices, Ween, East River Pipe, and, of course, Elliot Smith. Ok, there are songs here that will be used for her ‘90s Rock Photographs exhibit in Ontario. Cool. BASS WOMB ROOM: My ‘90s 4-Track Demos x Field Recordings by Melissa Auf der Maur California’s V Torres might leave you a little confused with her new release, the Woman E.P, which is a bit more than what it seems. On her debut release, V Torres seems to be suffering an identity crisis. Listening to the title track alone, there’s a strengthened Americana feel shuffling about, which gives listeners an idea of where Torres might be headed. It’s strong in the jangled guitars, the spaghetti western-styled guitar notes, and rhythm. Again, the force is strong with this one, and Torres is no slouch.  There’s a shift from track to track in her particular sound though, which bounces around through varying subgenres. Now, for most artists, this would be a problem many wouldn’t be able to get over quickly, but here, Torres rolls with the punches, never allowing it to become an issue. She hits with a 1-2 punch of “Winter Solstice,” filled with crunchy guitars and an 80s giving-no-fucks attitude. It’s sharp and direct. But it’s the simple and easy-flowing rhythm of “Great Escape” that’s captivating. There’s no grande flamboyance, just a catchy rhythm with an alluring melody and Torres’ voice knitting it all together. The most evident thing about V Torres throughout Woman is her honesty. She can rock out or coo you softly, and there isn’t anything fraudulent about it or her. She delivers it straight from the heart. Woman by V TORRES What? WHAT??? Ok, don’t get your panties in a bunch because it isn’t easy to surprise music aficionados. But then there’s a moment that slides past when you need to exclaim how you’re just completely fascinated by how the moment has shifted over the past four years and simply wonder, “How the hell did you get to this place?” But the question is rhetorical and far-fetched when we’re focused on what’s at hand: reimagining oneself yet remaining true to the artistry focal point. And this is where we are. Mykki Blanco’s 2022 Stay Close To Music was an amazing piece of work, and Blanco remained a favorite of mine for a couple of years, drifting from memory considering we hadn’t heard any new music, and I doubted we’d get anything. That all changed with the release of Café Paradiso (Transgressive) an album that sees Blanco moving in varying directions. While Stay Close rarely strayed from Blanco’s laid-back hip-hop, poised with unnerving skill and style, Blanco’s voice was welcoming, inviting, in a world that continued to be dominated by braggadocious emcees flaunting whips & chains. Oh, don’t get it twisted, Blanco doesn’t stray from flaunting anything, but cat walks right through the crowd. One might even say Blanco is very demure. Initially, I didn’t know where Blanco was heading, but of course, I’m willing to take the ride. Café Paradiso opens with the R&B-induced “Little Feet,” where vocals – which include Ian Isiah & Breakaway – aren’t raised above conversational voices. Here, the beat and low keys sweep across this canvas of sound and barely force any notes to land as addictively as they do. But the track doesn’t prepare you for what’s to follow with “NYC DOGS,” a quick-paced, grooving thrasher which allows Blanco to spread his wings into other directions through distortion, guitars, and noise, which sets the tone for his occasional maniacal vocal delivery. There’s such clever wording here though, beginning with “Jesus if you love me, where’s my fuckin money?/ Cuz the devil always pays on time,” which will make every Christian think for a sec before clamoring back, “I rebuke you demon!” But Blanco makes his move, addressing the audience for an interactive experience. What’s interesting is the sax that makes its way through halfway through the mix and sounds like it’s on the DL, barely noticeable but present. Ok so this is followed by “BUTT SEX,” which, ahem, yeah, just might be about what you think it’s about. Another interactive moment where Blanco exclaims how he needs all his “Baddies to the floor,” and adds, “No uglys, only baddies, uglys please exit the floor.” No minced wording here, but hot damn if that bouncy rhythm, that beat isn’t ever so enticing. “Easy Does It,” we find Mykki Blanco gliding through familiar territory, albeit slightly foreign, as words fly around this sultry beat with the keys repetitively sliding underneath. A dreamy R&B focal point that subtly plays with dynamics. Benét, not Eric, is featured here, but his voice and cadence don’t seem to fit the pattern or route Blanco has set. It isn’t bad, just doesn’t seem to fit. We get back what we came here to find, and that’s the Hip-Hop lyricism we’ve come to love. When I write “we,” yeah, I’m the we I’m talkin’ about. But hot damn! There’s a fire here, and that blaze is set off with “Hey Dopeman.” Rumors of Blanco’s demise have been highly exaggerated, and all comers can get it! Mykki is chillin, with Henny in hand, and completely flossed out. The flow, it’s mad ill, contorted and controlled, filled with metaphors, and the Morenito Chulo will not be denied! The Dona Blanco is winning, and there’s no doubt it, set to a backdrop that’s an ode to that old Boom-Bap, but rooted within the contemporary. There are other moments Blanco moves through pop culture, like the guitar-driven “Cut Me Open,” the rocking “Spread For Me,” and Euro-pop of “Wasted In Soho,” which I wanted to mention because there’s so much territory trodden through and maneuvered really well. It’s “Tough Guy” I wanted to delve into though, which for some reason makes me think of an American Peaky fookin’ Blinders. Maybe replace Cave with Blanco, and let the Bad Seeds do their own thing. Once again, it’s those repetitive keyboard notes accentuated by the deep bass line and drawn-out guitar. The music allows Blanco to bring out his inner P. Roger Nelson, not in sound & cadence but in sheer attitude. I’m exhausted, and the culprit is one Mykki Blanco. Café Paradiso shows Blanco as a multifaceted artist who is able to conceal, or rather, change musical stylings, like a chameleon can, and does, in forest settings. Blanco’s forest is much more urban but can shift from community to community with ease. CAFE PARADISO by Mykki Blanco Memories of LES, walking from local record stores downtown on St. Marks to Tompkins Square Park, getting a dirty water hot dog on the way. Hardly any cash in pockets, but we’d bum a cigarette from someone now and again. But we’d scrounge up enough money for a burger over at 7A, on 7th and, yeah, Avenue A. Those were days without Flock or Axon cameras, leaving no proof or evidence behind. Cop Shoot Cop, it’s another distant memory, left circling my head, but I did catch them live towards the end of its existence. Switching over to a major label back then was a long shot for a band that’s made its mark independently, but it was happening more often. But it’s only part of the story; the rest follows after the dissolution and the remaining member, after Tod A.’s departure, continuing, this time as Red Expendables, a copy handed to me by drummer Phil Puleo at a showcase of other bands. The group also released a single in 2024. They reworked songs to fit where they were heading, and while many continued on to work and create other outlets for themselves, the members continued to strike forward. This leads us to where we are now, years away from the past and into the future with EXP, the project centered on main players, AE Csaky (guitars/synth) and ex-CSC’s J. Natz (bass guitar/vocals). The band’s 12-song, self-titled debut (Reptilian Records) seems to wrap itself around repetition and rhythm, with the occasional tin-can-like percussion, which isn’t unusual if you’re familiar with the style and flow. It’s a very Lower East Side antic often played by creatives at one time, and it’s welcomed. “Armagedinstructionals” is a clear example in every sense, creating that trashy pattern for the repetition of guitar and bass. But it might just be one aspect of the group’s sound; it’s also Natz’ weathered voice that keeps you intrigued. On “Havok On The Astral,” he pushes to its limits. Mind you, it isn’t much different now than it was in the past, just slightly rougher. But again, the band melds its instruments in repetitive motions with a catchy melody that does the job it’s supposed to. There are moments though, when the repetition becomes repetitious but those are sometimes far and fleeting. “Isle Of Skye” though is different, and while it continues the same path, the instrumental lacks nothing. The bassline doesn’t stray from the course set, while strings tilt and whirl around the rhythm. What’s probably meant to be background noise is more of a shifting dreamscape that will eventually find its way embedded in your head. But this seems to be the point of the release, offering listeners a chance to feel the throbbing emotion underneath it all, slipping across its iteration that soothes at just about every turn. “Radiant One,” another instrumental, gives that. Guitars utilize the foundation of the rhythm to wrap notes around the composition. EXP is interesting in its delivery as the group allows the music to find its own way, exploring its own sound, fitting it with melody and a throbbing bottom end. EXP by EXP After a decade of silence since releasing a 7” single, and 12 years since the group’s last album, Electric Brick Wall, Black Bananas returns with a new album. For those not in the know, Black Bananas is made up of former RTX members Brian McKinley, Jennifer Herrema, and Kurt Midness, who were setting out to look for something new and fresh. Yes, I’m sure the irony in the group’s name doesn’t escape anyone. Through the band’s new release, Bad Bunch (Fire Records), Black Bananas dives deeper into experimentation, if such a thing is possible. That experimentation is littered with songs that are tinged with funk, 70s-styled R&B, and pop treatments that ravage musical cultures, only to deliver something so energetic and palpable that anyone and everyone can enjoy it. Ok, I’m getting ahead of myself here, but as “Cold Bussin’” leans in, it’s the rhythm – those bass and drum patterns that lay the groundwork for guitar effect-laden instrumentation, Hip-Hop vocal samples, and Herrema’s ethereal vocal delivery floating all around it. The air is thick and your steps might be sluggish as your body moves around this composition. It’s layered with as much as the band could get in; that wall of guitar and effects is noisy and captivating at the same time but it’s Herrema’s voice, in front and in the back, that steers things to their final resting point. No two songs are the same though, and “All The Way” is a testament to that. The skewed pop song with an infectious melody, whose lyrics you can barely make sense of, is a banger! The keys strewn about are laced with juicy notes, clashing against an odd beat and stormy effects. It delights the senses while at the same time, intrigues your thoughts on WTF the group is actually doing here. “Outta My Head” has effected vocal treatments over a mechanical beat, with a keyboard drifting all around it as washes of noisy melodies make their way in and out. This one is weird AF but addictive as sounds clash and collide. Things here are never what they seem. It’s the same with “Turkey Burgers,” which sometimes seems to defy the laws of gravity as the wash of keyboards allows it to stay in a constant state of flux, no corporeal form but lifted, atmospheric almost. The distant guitars are a sweet touch, coming close to the ground but PSYCH! It’s in the clouds baby. It’s groovy, swishing all around, leaving nothing to chance but at the same time allowing for happy accidents.  You might be left drowning in the creating that is “Eddie’s Album,” which is might have you throwing on your roller skates and cruising down to the park with your Walkman on, along with a couple of extra cassettes. It holds that vibe together with its deep bass, careening guitars & keyboards, with Herrema’s voice steadily focused on top. One thing about Black Bananas, throughout Bad Bunch, they’ll have you nostalgic while at the same time questioning yourself and your choices because yes, the group has taken a different approach, a different path to create such an exquisite collision of sound, yet there you are sitting in a cubicle.
