title: This One-Off V-10-Swapped Ford Mustang Avoided the Crusher. It’s Preserved as a 510-HP Middle Finger - Car and Driver
content: Kept hidden from Ford's bean counters for years, this 1999 GT still packs a serious 10-cylinder punch. Over the years, the Ford Mustang has been offered with four cylinders, six cylinders, and eight cylinders. A V-10 stuffed in a ‘Stang? No, at least not in a production model. However, in the early 2000s, a team of engineers at the Blue Oval’s Powertrain Research and Advanced Engines did just that. And they didn't ask permission first. That car—a silver 1999 GT coupe that had formerly served as a fitment mule for the naturally aspirated 5.4-liter V-8 Cobra R—found itself the recipient of one heck of a transplant. Displacing 5.8 liters, the 10-cylinder engine was completely unrelated to the Triton V-10 found in Ford’s truck applications; it was actually a 4.6-liter DOHC V-8 with two additional cylinders grafted on. Let’s restate that. The all-aluminum V-10 in this one-off Mustang was made by cutting up sand-casting molds for a 4.6-liter V-8, retooling those molds in a 10-cylinder format, then pouring in the molten aluminum. The motor got some Cobra parts, including connecting rods and pistons, but received its own billet crankshaft and overall weighed some 60 pounds less than the Cobra’s V-8. Power? Back in 2004, it made about 426 hp at 6500 rpm, a stout figure for its time and capable of running down the dragstrip in the high-11-second range. Best part? The team that built this car didn’t tell management they were working on it; they simply produced it as a fait accompli, the same trick Lamborghini’s engineers pulled on Ferruccio with the prototype Miura. Based on the displacement, the team started calling it the Boss 351. Unfortunately, Ford is not a small-batch Italian exotic automaker, and it employs plenty of people who make sure the books balance. As it aged, the Boss 351 became the oldest prototype on the books, and to hear some of the original build team tell the story, the accountants wanted it off the books. As in: sent to the crusher. Thus began a years-long cat-and-mouse game between those who loved this wild one-off and Ford's Vehicle Controls team, who were trying to find out where it had been stashed. Happily, after being tucked away in various hidden corners, the Boss 351 eventually came into the orbit of Ford's Heritage Fleet, who ensured it would be kept safe from being cubed. Now, the Heritage Fleet team has worked with the original build crew to return this V-10 Mustang back to its original glory. It needed new electronics and a thorough going-over, after which it was strapped to the dyno to see what the numbers said. Like a fine wine, apparently a V-10 Mustang improves with age, pushing over 510 horsepower at the wheels, with a soundtrack halfway between a bar brawl and a Lexus LFA. As a semi-secret project that survived only thanks to the enthusiasts in Ford's vast corporate structure, this one-of-one pony car has a great backstory. The fact that it's a relatively unremarkable SN95 Mustang with nearly double the power of a contemporary V-8-powered GT just makes it even cooler. Perhaps the best part is that it’s basically a sleeper, nondescript silver on five-spoke alloy wheels, nothing special until it clears its throat. Should Ford have built a 10-cylinder Mustang? The good news is that it did build at least one. The even better news is that the V-10 Boss 351 is still around. We may earn a commission for purchases made through our links.

title: Gasperini speaks to the media on the eve of Roma v Atalanta - AS Roma
content:
How is Paulo Dybala doing? Are there any opportunities in the free agents’ market and could Anass Salah-Eddine be brought back into the squad? “Nothing out of the ordinary. The tests didn’t show anything. He’ll be training today. The important thing is that he feels confident and comfortable because we’ve got three games this week. They’re all important fixtures and we need to be on top form. As for the free agents’ market, I think it’ll be difficult. I don’t know what the possibilities may be, but I wouldn’t count on it too much. Salah-Eddine has had a lot of opportunities, all of which he’s turned down. As for Roma, I’ve already made my choices and he’s not part of my plans.” Donyell Malen is on fire. He’s been compared to Gonzalo Higuain, but where can he improve? “He’s fine as he is, come on! Has he scored any headers? Maybe not. That’s missing from his repertoire. He’s scored with both his right and left foot so let’s see (laughs – ed.)” Is this the first real test to see if Roma have gained the experience needed to hold their own in head-to-head clashes? “Rather than a test of maturity, which this team has already shown it possesses, it’s a test of strength and quality. With the fixture list, we’re facing lots of top-of-the-table teams in the first 10-12 matchdays. I’d also consider Fiorentina as a quality side and winning away at Lecce is never easy. In the coming matches we’ll face not just Atalanta but also Inter, Como, and Napoli. In short, we have all these matches in the first half of the season, as well as the Champions League. That’s fine, it’s a journey and we’ll take it one step at a time, starting tomorrow when we’ll face a team of the highest calibre who have made a strong start. It’s a match that could decide our European fate.” How is Rodrigo Mora coming along? Do we need to get used to these ups and downs and the competition with Matias Soule? “He’s played two games in two. Whether he’s in the starting XI or on the bench, it’s not that someone who starts is a starting XI player and someone that gets subbed on is a substitute. It’s true that he’s young but he’s already shown he’s talented in the games against Fiorentina and Lecce. He’s very young and has plenty of room to grow in terms of his physical condition, stamina and endurance. We’re dealing with a player of exceptional quality – that’s hard to deny.” Can we expect any changes, or can we expect them for the third game this week? “We need to take it match by match. It’s true that these games are all close together but it’s impossible to predict what will happen on the pitch. We’ve gone months with no injuries, but when you start playing in the league and then the Champions League too, a few players are bound to pick up knocks. We just have to hope they’re not serious injuries. You can plan to rest one player or another, but it doesn’t always work that way. What I try to do is if someone is tired, I’ll bring on someone who’s in great form. Some decisions are made with that in mind. We can’t always say that a player has had a bump. But when there are longer-term injuries, there’s not much we can do.” Has Evan Ndicka recovered? Can you say anything about Lorenzo Pellegrini’s recovery? “Ndicka is a lot better. I think he can play. We’ll try him in training today. Pellegrini? He’s started to work with the group a bit. As for playing a match, maybe against Inter or after the break.” Will you be discussing a future together at dinner with Francesco Totti? “Absolutely not. I feel free to spend time with people that share knowledge, stir my emotions or who I just enjoy being with. There’s no ulterior motive. And it’s a freedom that I allow myself.” In an interview with La Gazzetta dello Sport, you mentioned that for many years Atalanta finished above Roma, then you arrived and Roma finished above them. Are you the deciding factor or have the two teams changed? “Atalanta have improved over the years and have finished above not only Roma, but several other teams as well. There have been many close encounters in the last few matchdays that have determined the league table, a bit like what happened last year. The coach plays a part, but it is always the complexity of the environment and the team that makes the difference. The team was exceptional last season. We were always close to fourth place, but the end of the season determined the outcome.” In the deal to bring in Marten De Roon, a player you know very well, following Neil El Aynaoui’s departure, was there also a sort of safeguard for Niccolo Pisilli? “Pisilli is well ahead. He’s matured, gained self-awareness, he’s grown and he’s a strong player. I’ve got four players there. I don’t do hierarchies. De Roon, [Leonardo] Balerdi and the new signings need to get into peak condition. They’ll come on for spells, and we’ll probably see them play a full game after the international break because they haven’t been here long. Pisilli, [Manu] Kone and [Bryan] Cristante are solid – there’s no hierarchy there. If someone’s fatigued, then whoever’s in better shape will play, as I said before. Maybe in a month’s time someone else will play more but they’re all part of the game regardless. We’ve got 16 players and there are lots of matches. Don’t make any distinctions between those that start and those who come on because, in the end, you’ll see that playing time will be similar for everyone.” The way you talk about your team, it sounds like you're in love with them. “That's true. This is a place you're happy to come to. We spend several hours a day here and when you have an atmosphere like this – where there are no disagreements and no one who is unlikeable – it's incredible to see how happy everyone is to train, even in the heat and despite the fatigue. That's down to the players. Regardless of our results, this is a very wholesome environment.” Against a four-man defence you usually field two strikers and a trequartista. Could Santiago Castro and Donyell Malen both start together – not just tomorrow – and could Rodrigo Mora play as a striker? “Sure. They're all versatile players who can adapt to different tactical systems. The more Castro and Mora play, the better they'll be able to fit into the team but there are no problems with the other players either.” Do you have a plan to make it harder for Atalanta to keep the ball? Possession play has always been key to Maurizio Sarri's game. “Atalanta are a great team, a top team, and they've strengthened considerably this summer, bringing in some big players such as [Franck] Kessie and [Jonathan] Rowe. They have a Champions League squad with strong alternatives and reliable players. The new coach will need a bit of time but everyone knows how good Sarri is. They've got off to a good start and that will help him too.” How is Matias Soule physically and mentally? And does the decision not to bring in a free agent regard only the left forward? “Soule’s groin injury is a distant memory. He’s made an outstanding recovery and he’s doing well. As for the transfer market, I’ve already talked about that. We’ll think about it, but overall, I don’t expect much.” Is there anything, throughout this experience at Roma, that has changed you as a coach? “This experience has certainly taught me a lot. I arrived at a different type of club after nine years of great achievements where I developed a strong sense of belonging to the city and the club. It wasn’t an easy decision, but I’m happy with it because I could no longer stay there. I am, however, extremely grateful and have the utmost respect for Atalanta. Rome has been the best place for me to feel alive again. It motivates you and we had to make the team better, so we had this challenge of improving on what had been done up to that point.” © 2018-2026 A.S. title: Brentford v Sunderland Premier League team news: Keith Andrews provides Mathias Jensen update - Brentford FC
content: “No, he won’t be back,” head coach Keith Andrews confirmed. “He has a little issue. He’ll miss this week and possibly next week. “We’ll see how he settles over the next couple of weeks. It’s nothing serious, but he certainly won’t be available for tomorrow.” Andrews reported no fresh injury concerns following the Bees’ trip to Elland Road. “The usual knocks and bruises, as you’d imagine with the level of game we had at Leeds,” he said. “The players have recovered well and trained well. We’re in a really good place.” While no new issues emerged from the trip to Leeds, Josh Dasilva sustained a hamstring injury during Brentford Under-21s’ 5-1 victory over Sunderland earlier this week. “That’ll knock Josh out until the international break,” Andrews explained. “It’s nothing too serious, but it’s obviously disappointing for him as he’s making his way back to that type of level, intensity and the performance levels he needs to get to. “That takes a little bit of time from where he’s been and the time out he’s had. It’s disappointing for him, we’re disappointed, but we’ll keep going and keep pushing Josh to get back to that level.” Sepp van den Berg, meanwhile, is expected to return after the international break as he continues his rehabilitation from a groin injury. “Sepp is making really good progress,” said Andrews. “He’s been back on the grass for the last week or 10 days, so he’s getting there. “He’s in a good place to come back after the international break. That’s realistic.” Antoni Milambo has stepped up his recovery from an anterior cruciate ligament injury and could feature for Brentford B in the coming weeks. “Antoni’s looking really good,” Andrews added. “He’s moving well. He was involved in an 11 v 11 on Wednesday, which was his first involvement in that type of scale and intensity, and on that size of pitch. “He recovered well from that and trained with us again this morning. title: Real Betis v Real Madrid: Match preview | La Liga - Yahoo Sports
content: Real Madrid will go back top of La Liga if they avoid defeat to Real Betis on Friday, but the goal will be to claim another victory at the start of the 2026-27 season. Jose Mourinho's side have won three from three so far, although the trip to La Cartuja will be their toughest test. After a slow start in the narrow victory over Espanyol two weeks ago, Real Madrid have built up steam well in the wins against Real Sociedad and Malaga. Eight goals have been scored across those two matches at the Bernabeu, and the challenge will be to continue that goalscoring form in Seville. Betis' defence can certainly be got at by Real Madrid, but concern will be the midfield battle. Isco is set to start against his former club, and he will be the talismanic figure that Los Verdiblancos look to play everything through, while Marc Cucurella must also shut down Antony if Mouringo's side are to be successful. Trips to the green-and-white side of Seville have been difficult for Real Madrid in recent years. 2021 (0-1, Dani Carvajal goal) was the last time a Los Blancos side were victorious in an away fixture against Betis, with three draws and a defeat since. Mourinho will be keen to end this unwanted run on Friday, although it will be easier said than done. The trio of Jude Bellingham, Vinicius Junior and Kylian Mbappe will be Real Madrid's go-tos for this one, and if even two of them are on form at La Cartuja, the chances of the three points returning to the Spanish capital will be high. But it will be just as important to keep things tight in defence too, especially with the quality that Betis have going forward.

title: ‘President v. President’: A pickleball showdown for the ages - The Lafayette – The Oldest College Newspaper in Pennsylvania
content: As the sun beamed down in 86-degree heat, nearly 50 students and staff piled under the trace of shade offered by Simon’s Market, waiting for the main event of Tuesday afternoon: “Presidential Pickleball.” Student Government hosted a pickleball event to open the multi-use sports court outside of Fisher Hall. The first game was the highlight: college President Nicole Hurd vs. Student Government President Allie Waxman ‘28. “I’m here, I’m about to lose to Allie, I think,” Hurd said, addressing the crowd. “That’s OK, I’m taking one for the team.” After Sen. Will Bennett ‘28 explained the rules regarding boundaries to Hurd and Waxman and a brief conversation about who would serve first (secretary Hayden Cohen ‘29 asked Waxman if she was serving, to which she triumphantly replied that she was, indeed, serving), the match to seven points began. Despite Hurd’s disclaimer, she got off to a hot start, winning the first four points of the match. After one of Hurd’s points, Cohen announced to the crowd via microphone that Waxman was a state champion in tennis in the state of New York. “I had no idea that she was a New York state champion tennis player,” Hurd said. “I’m glad I didn’t. That would’ve intimidated me more.” While Hurd kept working Waxman side to side, the Student Government President found her rhythm, returning Hurd’s low bounces with fire en route to six straight points. “President Hurd, you’re so good at pickleball,” Waxman said after one point in the match, a sense of bewilderment evident in her voice. The sixth straight Waxman point was a crushing one for Hurd, who whiffed on a slice to return the ball. Facing match point, Hurd mounted a resistance, keeping rallies alive, working both sides of the court, as Waxman began mounting errors of her own: a shot out of bounds and missing the ball on a low-placed shot from Hurd. Tied 6-6, the game was extended to win-by-two rules. Until the score reached 8-8, and both sides agreed enough was enough. One more point. Winner takes all. “I just felt like I, for Student Government, I needed to really push to take this win because this court was such a win,” Waxman said. Hurd served the ball in play. The closing lyrics of “Witchy” by Kaytranada and Childish Gambino played over the speaker (“Can you feel it?”) alongside a suspenseful bass drum. A shriek from Hurd after making contact with the ball. Nine seconds. Then, it was over. Hurd put a little too much mustard on the ball, hitting it out at the feet of Waxman, who was crowned the champion: 9-8. “I think I’m not gonna do another competition without some linesmen,” Hurd said jokingly. “I do have a competitive spirit. I also love our students, so I’m actually really happy with how that went,” she said. After the narrow win, Waxman stayed on the court, now accompanied by Bennett in a doubles match against Lafayette Activities Forum, taking on club president Lauren Finlay ‘27 and vice president of operations Fiona O’Connor ‘27, again in a game to seven. “I’ve never played pickleball before, so that was an experience,” Finlay said. Waxman noted that O’Connor played tennis in high school. Both sides traded blows in the early game, leading to a 4-4 tie. However, it was team Student Government that again came out on top, following a series of Lafayette Activities Forum errors and a backhand crusher from Waxman to seal the deal. “I think my confidence just wasn’t there at the beginning,” Finlay said. “They were already confident after their win. I wasn’t really there yet; this was my first time touching a racket.” Finlay and O’Connor proposed a rematch between the two organizations next week, this time in 3-on-3 basketball. title: Ipswich Town v Liverpool: Key stats and talking points - Yahoo Sports
content: BBC Sport examines some of the key themes before Friday's Premier League match (20:00 BST), with Liverpool heading to Suffolk in search of a first win under Andoni Iraola. Ipswich announced their 14th and final signing of the transfer window on deadline day, with striker Zian Flemming joining from Burnley. The Dutchman's arrival completed an unprecedented recruitment drive for the Blues, who have spent approximately £186m strengthening their squad. That surpasses the record for a newly promoted Premier League club in a single window, set by Sunderland last year, and also exceeds the summer outlay of European giants such as Barcelona and Paris St-Germain. Chairman Mark Ashton revealed last month that the club's US owners had instructed him to "go right to the limit of financial fair play". They are gambling that greater investment, coupled with a shift towards signing primarily overseas players, will help Town bridge the gulf in quality. Ipswich's spending has focused mainly on midfield and attacking reinforcements. Although former Fulham centre-back Issa Diop has come into the side, three of the back four who started this season's opening two league games were also first-choice when the Tractor Boys were relegated in 2024-25 and defence may be an area of weakness. That was certainly the case in last weekend's 5-2 defeat at Manchester United. After a competitive first half, Ipswich lost their way shortly after the restart, conceding twice in the space of three minutes. Gary O'Neil admitted his side lacked "emotional discipline" after United's second goal was allowed to stand despite Harry Maguire handling the ball in the build-up. Greater composure will be needed against opponents who usually dominate this fixture. The Tractor Boys have lost their last four league games against Liverpool, conceding 17 times and scoring just once, while it is 40 years since their last home victory over the Merseysiders. Liverpool came from behind twice to draw 2-2 with Nottingham Forest on Saturday, just as they did at Newcastle on the opening weekend. New boss Andoni Iraola, who failed to win any of his first nine Premier League matches as Bournemouth head coach, will hope it is third time lucky at Portman Road. The Spaniard said this week he was happy with his side's summer transfer business. The Reds' net spend was approximately £200m, the highest in the top flight, although the decision not to strengthen at full-back has come under scrutiny. More than half of the outlay went on former Paris St-Germain winger Bradley Barcola, who is available to make his Premier League debut. The 23-year-old did not come cheap, having joined for a fee of £107m that could rise to £123m, but has a combination of attributes that would appeal to any club seeking an elite goalscoring wide player. Barcola's best season to date came in 2024-25, when he scored or assisted 39 goals, the ninth-highest total by any player in Europe's top five leagues. While that figure fell to 21 last season, many of his underlying metrics remained impressive. Used primarily on the left flank, Barcola utilised his dribbling ability and pace to create shooting opportunities for himself. He was the only player in Europe's top five leagues to average more than two shot-ending carries per 90 minutes, defined as shots taken after carrying the ball for at least five metres. He also ranked highly for receiving the ball in dangerous areas, averaging nearly nine touches in the opposition box per 90 minutes. That placed him seventh among more than 1,500 eligible players, on a list headed by Barcelona star Lamine Yamal.

title: The Jensen Interceptor Returns as a 960-HP V-8 Track Monster, and Will Spawn Roadgoing Variants - Car and Driver
content: The new Interceptor GTX mirrors its ancestor’s fetching proportions and brings motorsports-inspired aerodynamics and a punchy V-8. Early this year, we learned of a surprising automotive revival. Jensen International Automotive, which had been busy restoring the classic Interceptor of the ’60s and ’70s, announced it was developing an all-new Interceptor GTX. This summer, the company teased the car again and said it would arrive first in track-only form. Now, Jensen International has fully unveiled the Interceptor GTX and hinted at how the GTX will translate into a road-going model. The Interceptor GTX’s spec sheet looks promising. Under the hood lies a supercharged V-8 sending 960 horsepower to the rear wheels. Based on an LT-series engine from General Motors, the V-8 has been heavily reengineered by Texas-based Late Model Engines, and fewer than 20 percent of the original GM components remain. The 6.8-liter engine can rev to 7000 rpm and is mated to a 2.7-liter Roots-type supercharger with electronic boost control, which Jensen International says provides rapid throttle response and linear power delivery. Modifications include CNC-machined heads, titanium valves, and reworked variable valve timing and direct-injection systems. Jensen says the engine is capable of up to 1200 horsepower and over 1000 pound-feet of torque. That muscle is sent to the rear transaxle via a carbon-fiber driveshaft that sits within a steel torque tube. The six-speed sequential transmission from Samsonas Motorsport features straight-cut dog gears, and the driver can shift either via steering-column-mounted paddles or a lever on the transmission tunnel. Jensen International says the future road-going Interceptors could use either an H-pattern manual transmission or an automatic gearbox. The Interceptor GTX uses steel brake rotors, and the brake balance is adjustable from within the cabin. Jensen International didn’t provide a curb weight, but says the all-aluminum chassis creates a rigid structure while keeping weight down. It’s complemented by an aluminum unequal-length control-arm suspension with three-way manually adjustable dampers. The Interceptor GTX also uses a hydraulic power-assisted steering rack, and it rides on forged-aluminum one-piece Vossen 20-inch wheels wrapped in Michelin Pilot Sport 4S tires. The styling references the original Interceptor without being a faithful recreation. The GTX follows its forebear’s dramatic proportions, with a long hood and a fastback roofline. Jensen International partnered with Avant Design, an independent studio that has also worked on the electric Longbow sports car and the LEVC TX that serves as London’s default taxi, and it recently shared a vision of a future Lotus sports car. The bodywork is handcrafted from aluminum by British specialists Coventry Metalcraft and is characterized by crisp, assertive lines. The front end reminds us of the Chevy Camaro, and the GTX’s motorsports focus makes it look like a more luxurious take on the NASCAR Garage 56 racer that took on the 24 Hours of Le Mans in 2023. The headlights sit within a thin, recessed band across the front end, with vertical, slanted LEDs sitting on either side of the grille. The roof is painted black, and the rear section of the cabin features a sizable glass panel, echoing the glass rear dome that made the original Interceptor stand out. The rear fascia features a simple LED full-width taillight. Aerodynamics play a key role on the GTX. The front bumper incorporates a large splitter below a trapezoidal intake, within which sits another carbon-fiber plane. A large slash behind the front wheels extracts hot air from the brakes, and the distinctive side skirts feature fins at the front and rear. A massive diffuser is integrated into the rear bumper, with the oval exhaust pipes positioned just above. And it’s impossible to miss the adjustable rear wing, which towers above the sloping glass and can generate over 771 pounds of downforce. The cabin looks like it came straight out of a race car, with a bespoke, FIA-approved roll cage, Tillett carbon-fiber seats, six-point harnesses, and a fire-extinguisher system. There’s a sizable digital display behind the steering wheel, but no central screen. Still, despite the stripped-back approach, Jensen International has fitted Alcantara-wrapped padding with orange stitching for a bit of added comfort. Jensen International describes the GTX as an “enhanced prototype,” but this radical track car will spawn street-legal Interceptors in the future, with the company also revealing its first images of these models. Jensen is planning an Interceptor GTR—essentially a roadgoing version of the GTX—and a more luxury-focused Interceptor GT. The images of the expanded family show a GT model with cleaner bodywork devoid of aerodynamic appendages and a GTR model that sits somewhere in between with a smaller wing and front splitter. The Interceptor GTX will now begin dynamic testing and evaluation, and Jensen says it will work with customers to tailor the vehicle specifications to each individual. There was no timeline provided for when the GTX might reach customers, nor when the GTR and GT models will launch. Jensen International has previously said the GTX would be available in the U.K. in "ultra-limited numbers,” but it’s unclear if those plans are still in place. Pricing is also yet to be announced, but we’re eager to learn more about this handsome revival of a classic grand tourer. Caleb Miller began blogging about cars at 13 years old, and he realized his dream of writing for a car magazine after graduating from Carnegie Mellon University and joining the Car and Driver team. He loves quirky and obscure autos, aiming to one day own something bizarre like a Nissan S-Cargo, and is an avid motorsports fan. We may earn a commission for purchases made through our links.

title: Defend Community Integration Coalition Statement on Texas v. Kennedy - DREDF
content: The Defend Community Integration Coalition is a coalition of national, state, and local organizations, allies, and individual advocates working together to protect the right of disabled people to live in our own homes and communities. Today, disabled people are part of community life. That was not always true. For decades, we were placed in institutions and cut out of family and community life. It changed because disabled people and our allies fought for it, winning laws like the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 and the Americans with Disabilities Act that establish our right to be included in our communities. Community integration means having the supports to fully participate at home, at work, and in the activities we enjoy, alongside our family, friends, and peers. It means no one is segregated or forced into an institution to get their needs met. That right is under direct attack. On August 31, 2026, the Department of Justice, on behalf of the Department of Health and Human Services, joined Alaska, Florida, Louisiana, Montana, and Texas in filing a proposed resolution of Texas v. Kennedy that asks the court to vacate the community integration provisions of the Section 504 regulations. The Coalition came together for exactly this moment, and we can fight for the future of community living together. The statement below is the Coalition’s response: The Defend Community Integration Coalition strongly condemns the recent proposed joint resolution filed August 31 in the ongoing case Texas v. Kennedy. The proposed resolution aims to strike down the 2024 community integration regulations under Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973. This action flies in the face of decades of judicial precedent and Congressional intent to ensure that community integration remains a civil right for all people with disabilities. As national disability rights leaders and allies, we have worked hard for decades to advance community integration as a foundational civil right for people with disabilities. We condemn any attacks aimed at undoing this work led by and for people with disabilities. For people with disabilities, there is no right more foundational than the right to make our own choices. Far too often, we find ourselves in the position where others decide our lives for us. It takes a lot to ensure that the choices we have are real choices. It has taken years to build the supports we need to go to school, work, eat, stay housed, and raise our children. As humans, we deserve the security of knowing that we have what we need to live our lives. Life is not just about getting three square meals a day and getting our meds on time. It is about growing, working, loving, dreaming, failing and reaching our potential. It is about deciding when to get up, when to go out, what to eat, and with whom to live. It is hard to do these things when we are forced to stay in congregate settings where we have no say over most aspects of our lives. Disabled people are survivors. We are spouses, parents, siblings, classmates, colleagues, and neighbors. Most of all, we are Americans determined to fight back against ideas and actions that take away our dignity and roll back years of hard-fought progress and rights. As a coalition we will continue to work together and fight for the full realization of the community integration mandate. Community integration of people with disabilities is non-negotiable. This is a monumental fight. In a moment like this we need to join forces and work collectively. We are stronger together. To join the Defend Community Integration Coalition, sign up here. Below are additional resources and calls to action: Defend Community Integration Coalition’s membership is comprised of Access Living, American Association of People with Disabilities, Autistic Self Advocacy Network, Bazelon Center for Mental Health Law, Caring Across Generations, Center for Public Representation, Disability Rights Education & Defense Fund, National Association of Councils on Developmental Disabilities, National Council on Independent Living, National Disability Rights Network, and United Spinal Association. Organizations that wish to join this coalition can sign up at ncil.org/community. title: UND Law Professor Carolyn V. Williams Honored for Scholarship, Elected to Third Term as LWI Treasurer - University of North Dakota (UND)
content: Updates from the University of North Dakota School of Law. University of North Dakota School of Law Professor Carolyn V. Williams presented twice at the 2026 Legal Writing Institute (LWI) Biennial Conference, where she also received the Teresa Godwin Phelps Award for Scholarship in Legal Communication and was elected to a third term as Treasurer of the organization. Williams’s first presentation, “Writing With AI, Writing About AI: The Dual Role of LRW Scholarship,” joined fellow legal writing scholars in examining the role generative artificial intelligence can play both in producing legal scholarship and as a subject of scholarly inquiry. Williams argued that scholars should be encouraged to use generative AI when it can assist with time-consuming aspects of the writing process, while emphasizing that scholars must remain responsible for the substantive expertise, analysis, judgment, and ideas underlying their work. She also addressed the distinction between citing AI as an authoritative source and acknowledging its use as a tool in the scholarly process. The second half of Williams’s presentation focused on emerging scholarship concerning AI and legal education. She encouraged legal writing scholars to consider how their existing areas of expertise intersect with the challenges AI is creating for legal education and practice. Williams also served as moderator for a work-in-progress presentation of Professor Richard Luedeman, “The AI Dilemma in Legal Education.” Her comments explored the intersection of generative AI, law-school assessment, and disability accommodations, building on questions raised in her own scholarship about how law professors should redesign assessments in response to AI and the NextGen bar exam. During the conference, Williams was presented with the 2025 Teresa Godwin Phelps Award for Scholarship in Legal Communication for her article, “Bracing for Impact: Revising Legal Writing Assessments Ahead of the Collision of Generative AI and the NextGen Bar Exam.” Presented by LWI, the national award recognizes outstanding scholarship that significantly advances the field of legal communication. Williams’s article examines the simultaneous changes brought about by generative AI and the NextGen bar exam and argues that law schools should rethink traditional legal writing assessments to better prepare students for modern legal practice. Williams was also elected to a third term as Treasurer of the Legal Writing Institute. LWI is a nonprofit organization dedicated to improving legal communication by supporting the development of teaching and scholarly resources and providing forums for discussion of the study, teaching, and practice of professional legal writing. With members from law schools throughout the United States and abroad, LWI is one of the largest organizations of legal academics in the country. title: Member Alert: New Handguns Added to California Roster Pursuant to Boland v. Bonta - California Rifle & Pistol Association
content:
For over a decade, California’s Unsafe Handgun Act froze the state’s handgun roster in place. The microstamping mandate, which took effect in 2013, made it virtually impossible for manufacturers to add new semiautomatic pistol models to the Roster of Certified Handguns. The roster shrank year after year. Californians were locked out of the same modern, reliable handguns available to law-abiding citizens in every other state. CRPA refused to accept that. And because of your support, the roster is growing again. Today, September 3, 2026, the California Department of Justice added 25 new semiautomatic handgun models to the Roster of Certified Handguns pursuant to the court’s order in Boland v. Bonta, CRPA’s federal lawsuit challenging the Unsafe Handgun Act. ·         M&P 10mm M2.0 (4.6” and 5.6” barrels, optics ready) ·         Bodyguard 2.0 .380 AUTO (7 configurations) Not a single one of these handguns would be available to California consumers without CRPA’s lawsuit. The full list is available at oag.ca.gov/firearms/certified-handguns/recently-added. In March 2023, Judge Cormac Carney of the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California granted CRPA’s motion for a preliminary injunction, finding that the Unsafe Handgun Act’s microstamping, chamber load indicator, and magazine disconnect requirements likely violate the Second Amendment under the U.S. Supreme Court’s framework in Boland v. Bonta. The court held that these requirements “generally prohibit Californians from acquiring state-of-the-art handguns” that are protected arms under the Second Amendment, and that the State failed to identify any historical tradition justifying those restrictions. The State appealed. The Ninth Circuit partially stayed the injunction, reinstating the chamber load indicator and magazine disconnect requirements while the appeal proceeds, but left the microstamping injunction in place. That injunction is the reason new semiautomatic pistols are reaching the California roster for the first time in over a decade. Following oral argument in August 2023, the Ninth Circuit held the case pending its en banc decision in Duncan v. Bonta. After Duncan was decided in March 2025, the court ordered supplemental briefing, which both sides completed in spring 2025. The appeal is now fully briefed and awaiting decision before the same 11-judge en banc panel. The fight is far from over. The microstamping injunction that opened the door for these new roster additions remains in effect only because of this litigation. If CRPA were not actively prosecuting Boland v. Bonta, the injunction could be dissolved and the roster would once again be frozen. CRPA continues to press for full invalidation of the Unsafe Handgun Act’s unconstitutional restrictions, including the chamber load indicator and magazine disconnect requirements that the Ninth Circuit temporarily reinstated. These requirements continue to block additional handgun models from reaching California consumers. A favorable ruling from the en banc panel would be a generational victory for California gun owners, striking down all three requirements and restoring meaningful access to modern, reliable handguns protected by the Second Amendment. Every new handgun on that roster exists because CRPA had the resources to take this fight to federal court and sustain it for years. Litigation of this magnitude costs hundreds of thousands of dollars. Your donations fund the attorneys, experts, and briefing that make victories like Boland possible. title: Cadillac V-One Concept Engineer Spills the Secrets of a Customer-Spec Le Mans Hypercar - The Drive
content:
We have updated our Privacy Policy. Please review to learn more. By continuing to use our services, you agree to these updates. Published				

					Sep 3, 2026 3:42 PM EDT Our free daily newsletter sends the stories that really matter directly to you, every weekday. Ask the nice folks at Cadillac about this slick prototype race car displayed at The Quail during Monterey Car Week, and they’ll tell you over and over again that it’s just a “design study,” a “concept,” a “race car project.” Ask folks who have their ears on the ground at paddocks across the globe, and they’ll tell you that the program to sell these simplified Le Mans racers to customers is just about finalized. That’s the best way to describe this beauty that Cadillac calls the V-One: an 830-horsepower, simplified Le Mans Hypercar—capital H because the real deal races in WEC’s Hypercar class (and IMSA’s GTP). And regardless of whether General Motors plans on selling these to a wider audience or just a select few—or even just one person like Porsche did for Roger Penske—the task of dumbing down one of the world’s most advanced race cars is no small feat. There’s the engine side, the hybrid side, the electronics, suspension, downforce, maintenance intervals that could quickly bankrupt a very wealthy person, and, last but not least, selling a vehicle that 99.9% of people don’t have the skills to drive is a challenge in and of itself. And for those who do have the skills, then there’s the problem of where do you drive it, and how big of an army of engineers do you need to operate it? Where do you store it, and how do you prep it to make sure it starts up again later? I spoke with Sean O’Shea, the lead propulsion engineer for Cadillac Racing and GM Motorsport’s hybrid powertrains, to get all of those answers and then some. He and I had the chance to explore the V-One up close and learn about what makes this project so ambitious, but also so exciting. Here’s how Cadillac is building a Le Mans Hypercar that anyone can jump in and drive: Jerry Perez: I know the official company line is that this is a concept, but what is Cadillac really trying to achieve here? Is the goal to just make a concept that never goes anywhere, or something that will become a reality? And how are you involved in all of this? Sean O’Shea: As the engineering representative linking the design and the racing program, I’m really trying to make sure that [V-One] doesn’t stray too far from the race-car side and that this could be a reality. It’s a concept now, but everything you see here is very feasible and could be a reality. I’m a big racing guy; I’ve been racing everything since I was little, like go-karts, cars, dirt bikes, all of it. I love racing, so when I got involved in the project, I wanted to make a track car that was a simplified version of our race car, but still had all the same tools and the same experience you would get as a pro driver, without being overly complicated. Race cars are known for being complicated, so how do you take a Le Mans racer and make it less complicated? Well, first, I want it to be a really fun track car, and one of the major details is that it needed to be an “ambient start car,” right? This means you can start it at 70 degrees and let it warm up on its own without having to pre-warm it [with auxiliary machinery like an F1 car]. Also, all the differential, traction control, and suspension are a simplified version of the real car. This means you can just go out and just drive the car and have a really good time. However, I didn’t want to take away from the sound, the power, or the downforce you have in a real race car. This way, when you get in it and look around, you get the same view as any of our pro drivers like Earl Bamber, Jack Aitken, or Delatraz. You’ll also have the same buttons around the cockpit, but maybe not all 12 control variations or whatever, right? That’s what I mean by the simplified version: something we mortals can learn, work through, and have a good time with. I once spoke with Jenson Button while he was racing the Acura ARX at the Rolex 24, and he flat-out told me that the steering wheel and some of the controls of the GTP car—as well as the rear axle, brake balance, and traction control—were more complicated than in an F1 car from his era. If he is saying that, I can’t imagine what a normal person would say. We had Jenson drive the [WEC] car, and yeah, the race car project is so complicated given what they want to accomplish. Between settings, energy recovery, and energy per lap, I worked with our pro drivers and just asked them: what would you like to simplify in the car if you wanted it to be fun? They gave me a lot of ideas, so if you look at the interior, it’s just an LMDh car, just a simplified version of it. We still have traction control with two settings—X and Y for lateral and longitudinal grip—and we really wanted to put ABS in the car, although these cars normally don’t have it. I wanted ABS to kind of eliminate the issues around break-in temperatures, tire warm-up procedures, and all of that. Just let the ABS handle it, then let the driver go out and learn to steer, shift, and go fast. We worked closely with the [pro] drivers to understand how we can reduce complexity. And on the propulsion side and differential side, we worked with all of our performance engineers to, again, learn how to simplify things. We went to Goodwood last year and this year, and it was like, how can the car be easy to use? You know, we started just kind of throwing calibration ideas out there, so that our driver could just basically drive out of the paddock and drive onto the track and not have a team of engineers with them. If you were to build this, would the driver just jump in and go? The idea would be that we jump in, start it, and go. Well, you have to let it warm up before you go anywhere, you know, give it a little care. This is expensive, after all. Would customers keep their cars at home, or would Cadillac store and transport them to tracks, as Ferrari does with its FXX program? We have ideas and a kind of plan, but it’s nothing we’re ready to divulge yet. But for me, being just an enthusiast, if I bought this, I would want to keep it at home and impress my neighbors. Who all has driven the V-One, and what’s their feedback so far? Our pro drivers are in it since this is really close to the race car. We engineers don’t really drive it at all. I’ve been in the seat and pushed it around on EV drive, but nothing more than that. I really draw on their experience because they also drive our road cars; they’ve helped with the ZR1X programs, and they spend a lot of time in the sim rig. Together, we really looked at the interior [cabin] space and explored how to make it a little bigger. So I was like, can we remove the sway bars? And they were like, no, we need adjustable sway bars. I said, okay, but do you just need the rear and not the front? And the drivers were like, you need both—so we kept both. That type of stuff. Which buttons did you keep on the dash and steering wheel, and what about the air conditioning? Yes, there’s AC inside the car. The race car gets very hot, so we knew we wanted to keep that. There’s also pit lane limiter and other buttons to adjust various settings we already discussed. You kept the loud bang from the transition from electric to ICE, like the race car when leaving pit lane, right? Right, we didn’t want to change any of that. Plus, these things are miserable at slow speeds, so it’s much easier to maneuver the car on electric power; then you can just drive around. Again, the idea is to make it simple to use. Start the car, let it warm up. When you pull out of the pits, the ICE engine shuts off, and you leave in EV. Then you let one of the paddles go, and it turns the ICE engine on, and you go. The interior, really. It’s the biggest change from the race car. We just want to make sure that we had space for a normal-sized human in there. And also visibility, because the race car is very claustrophobic. And we had to do all this without changing the tub shape, because if you change the tub, now you gotta make new tooling and homologate everything else. After that, it was just simplifying all the sensors and electronics. Whenever a car company announces an “F1 car for the road,” it usually ends up rather messy. Whether it’s the McLaren F1, the Mercedes-AMG One, you name it, they’re awesome, but they’re full of gizmos and maintenance and reliability nightmares. I know this isn’t an F1 car, but pretty darn close. Never driven an AMG One, but I’ve seen a lot about it, including on the forums. But to me, the complication just isn’t necessary. The core experience for me is being in the car, just having a good time, feeling the downforce, feeling the Gs, hearing the sound, and racing the car on a track. So, for everything we did here, I just wanted to simplify the race car and make it reliable and easy to use. The whole point is to give the owner the experience of driving the car, not to mess with gizmos, gadgets, screens, and everything else. Drive the car! What are maintenance intervals like on one of these? Anytime we do a performance car, anything inside GM, we start with a vehicle technical spec. So you put in what you want the car to do. right? Do you want to have good fuel mileage?  Do you want to have faster 0-60 or lap times, all that stuff? When I did the vehicle technical spec for this, we targeted a lap time—it was a little bit slower than in the race car, and I targeted our performance interval, which is our highest in GM, to 24 hours of just changing tires. So, for 24 hours of racing, just add fuel, change tires, and go. If you want to go out and run 24 hours, that’s what the car will need. Lastly, how will you gauge whether a potential customer can handle a V-One? Can someone who’s never driven a race car just jump in and have fun? That’s what I hope, and that applies to me too. I’ve driven a lot of stuff in my life, but I’ve never driven a full downforce car, so my ultimate goal is just to drive this and have a good time. title: Carmelite Sisters for the Aged and Infirm v. Prince - Becket — Religious Liberty for All
content: For nearly 175 years, Catholic healthcare ministries have cared for the sick, the elderly, and the dying across Illinois. Guided by the belief that every life is a precious gift, these ministries accompany those nearing death with medical skill, prayer, and love until God calls them home. But now Illinois is threatening them with significant fines and penalties unless they help patients obtain lethal suicide drugs—forcing Catholic hospitals, religious sisters, and healthcare professionals to violate their faith or abandon the very people they serve. For millennia, Catholics around the world have operated healthcare ministries to serve the sick and dying. Rooted in Christ’s command to care for the “least of these,” these ministries put their faith into practice by offering excellent medical care, spiritual support, sacramental care, and end-of-life accompaniment to the most vulnerable. Even when a patient is facing a terminal illness and cannot be cured, Catholic providers give their all to surround them with the greatest love imaginable, to alleviate their suffering, and to ignite in them a hope for the world to come. Illinois has long benefited from this compassionate service. For nearly 175 years, Catholic healthcare ministries have been a refuge for the sick, elderly, and dying across Illinois.  Today, that work includes Catholic hospitals treating millions of patients each year. It also includes the work of religious Sisters caring for the elderly, and faithful Catholic laypeople serving as healthcare professionals in every part of the state. Since 1964, the Carmelite Sisters for the Aged and Infirm have cared for elderly Illinoisans at St. Patrick’s Residence in Naperville, providing long-term, rehabilitative, and palliative care alongside daily prayer and loving presence—ensuring that no resident dies alone. The Little Sisters of the Poor first came to Illinois in 1876 to minister to those devastated by the Great Chicago Fire. Today, they continue caring for the elderly in Chicago and Palatine, where they accompany those they serve in a spirit of hospitality, companionship, and trust in God’s providence. That same commitment to healing has guided Luke Vander Bleek throughout his career as a pharmacist. For the past forty years, he has sought to use his pharmaceutical skills to serve and heal his community, all motivated by his Catholic faith. He currently runs a community pharmacy in Morrison, Illinois, a town of 4,000 two hours west of Chicago. Illinois tries to strong-arm nuns into its regime of death In 2026, Illinois passed its End-of-Life Options for Terminally Ill Patients Act (EOLOA), allowing terminally ill adults to obtain lethal drugs to end their lives. Yet the law does not merely permit assisted suicide: it forces objecting healthcare providers into its machinery. Religious providers who object to participating in assisted suicide must still inform patients about their “right” to kill themselves, help them qualify for lethal drugs, and pass them along to someone willing to help them obtain those drugs. Meanwhile, pharmacists like Vander Bleek must fill lethal prescriptions or refer patients to another pharmacy that will. In other words, Illinois makes religious healthcare providers punch the patient’s ticket to death even when doing so violates their faith. Illinois also imposes a gag order on religious caregivers who want to speak a life-affirming message against suicide. EOLOA’s definition of coercion and undue influence is so broad that it risks punishing the Sisters and healthcare providers in the Archdiocese simply for telling a suffering patient, “Don’t kill yourself. Jesus loves you. Your life is precious.” Catholic teaching forbids the Archdiocese’s healthcare ministries, the Sisters, and Vander Bleek from prescribing life-ending drugs, directing patients to obtain them, or helping facilitate a patient’s suicide in any way.  The Church teaches that when a person is suffering deeply, the proper response is loving accompaniment—not abandonment to death.Rather, they accept death as the natural end to a life well-lived: to accept it as it comes, neither artificially hastening it through any means, nor artificially prolonging it through burdensome technological and medical advancements that provide no reasonable benefit. Catholic ministries fight for their freedom to care With Becket’s help, Cardinal Cupich, the Carmelite Sisters, the Little Sisters, and Vander Bleek filed a federal lawsuit seeking to block Illinois’ assisted-suicide law before it takes effect on September 12, 2026. The lawsuit asks the court to protect their freedom to continue caring for the sick, elderly, and dying in accordance with their Catholic faith. The lawsuit also seeks to protect the rights of patients who want the freedom to choose care providers who will not offer them suicide. Illinois’ actions violate core constitutional protections for religious freedom and freedom of speech. The government cannot force Catholic ministries and healthcare professionals to violate their faith by helping patients obtain suicide pills. Nor can it gag Catholic doctors, nurses, caregivers, and pharmacists from offering life-affirming counsel and force them instead to deliver the state’s preferred message about suicide. Federal law further protects these providers by banning the use of federal health care funds for assisted suicide and by forbidding Illinois from discriminating against those who, like Becket’s clients, refuse to participate in assisted suicide. For generations, Catholic healthcare ministries have offered the sick and dying across Illinois a place of peace, prayer, and love at the end of life. Illinois should stop trampling religious freedom and forcing its message of death on vulnerable patients. Subscribe to receive our monthly newsletter and breaking news updates.

title: Commonwealth v. Anyssa M. Allen - City of Norfolk (.gov)
content: NORFOLK, Va. — Anyssa Michelle Allen, 31, was sentenced on July 31 to serve one month in jail after a jury convicted her in May of second-offense misdemeanor driving under the influence when police found her vehicle crashed into a bush in early 2024. After 2:30 a.m. on Jan. 28, 2024, Ms. Allen was driving drunk and crashed into a bush near the intersection of Shore Drive and Pretty Lake Avenue. A Norfolk Police patrol officer saw Ms. Allen’s vehicle, pulled over, and checked on Ms. Allen. When Ms. Allen got out of her vehicle, the officer noticed that she smelled of alcohol. Ms. Allen agreed to take field sobriety tests, in which she displayed unsteadiness, and after being transported to Norfolk City Jail, she agreed to a breath alcohol test, which indicated that she had a blood-alcohol concentration of 0.13 (well over the legal limit of .08). Ms. Allen had been convicted of a previous DUI in Hanover County in 2015, and so the police charged her with misdemeanor second-offense DUI within 10 years. This crime, under Virginia law, carries mandatory minimum penalties of a $500 fine and 10 days in jail. Ms. Allen stood trial for her charge in Norfolk General District Court in May 2025, was convicted, and appealed her conviction to Norfolk Circuit Court, opting to be tried by a jury. At her jury trial on May 21, 2026, Ms. Allen claimed in her defense to have been drugged (or “roofied”) on the night of the crash. After hearing the evidence and arguments from the Commonwealth and Ms. Allen’s defense counsel, the jury rejected this claim and convicted Ms. Allen as charged. Judge Devon R. Paige, who presided over the trial, set Ms. Allen’s sentencing hearing on July 31. After hearing sentencing arguments from the Commonwealth and the defense, Judge Paige sentenced Ms. Allen to serve one month in jail and to pay a $500 fine. Judge Paige suspended an additional 11 months in jail on the conditions that Ms. Allen obeys the law for 12 months, completes an education course through the Virginia Alcohol Safety Action Program, and has her driving privileges suspended for three years. “A crime does not have to be a felony to be serious,” said Commonwealth’s Attorney Ramin Fatehi. “Ms. Allen may have committed ‘only’ a misdemeanor, but her actions endangered herself and other people on the road. Having committed this crime before, Ms. Allen should have known better, and that is why she has gone to jail for it, and I hope that the rehabilitative program in VASAP will help her put this conduct behind her. No matter what the crime, my prosecutors and I will continue to make safety and fairness our highest priorities as we look for appropriate accountability in our city.” Assistant Commonwealth’s Attorneys William D. Cox and Tara Sue Terwilliger prosecuted Ms. Allen’s case in Circuit Court, Assistant Commonwealth’s Attorney Chandler W. Holcomb tried Ms. Allen’s case in General District Court, and Norfolk Police Detective (then-officer) Logan T. Gardner led the investigation.

title: V162: Crafting Joy With Anya Taylor-Joy - V Magazine
content: From the world of Dune to the high-stakes suspense of Lucky, the actor is turning the page to a bold new chapter. Dressed in bespoke paper creations by fashion’s latest visionaries, the actor reminds us that the most compelling narratives are crafted with equal parts imagination and style From the world of Dune to the high-stakes suspense of Lucky, the actor is turning the page to a bold new chapter. Dressed in bespoke paper creations by fashion’s latest visionaries, the actor reminds us that the most compelling narratives are crafted with equal parts imagination and style The nature of paper is that it’s always in a state of becoming: a story, a journal, a script, and now, a dress. Few know this better than Anya Taylor-Joy, whose own love of the written word has inspired a monumental creative dialogue between V, photographer Nick Knight, stylist Anna Trevelyan, a coterie of designers, and Montblanc, known for their own dedication to the life of a page. For the September issue of V, the likes of Matthew David Andrews, Noel Stewart, Jenny Beattie, AGRO Studio, Macy Grimshaw, Thevxlley, Gaurav Gupta, Miguel Castro Freitas for Mugler, and Zac Posen for GapStudio produced original dresses made entirely of paper for Taylor-Joy to wear. In a world that’s increasingly so digital, there’s ever more beauty in the tactile. This collaboration becomes a love letter to fashion, punctuated with the words “I love you my angel,” written by Taylor-Joy’s own mother in Montblanc’s Meisterstück pen when she visited the set of the photoshoot. No matter the folds and creases of life, Taylor-Joy has come to see the world through pages of her own, whether as a longtime keeper of journals; an avid reader; on scripts she helps bring to life as an actor in films like Dune’s third installment, arriving later this year; or as a producer, on series like Lucky and movies like Sacrifice. As she continues writing the chapters of her life, Anya Taylor-Joy spoke to dear friend Miley Cyrus for V about building a character, escaping the pressures of fame, managing expectations, and finding the beauty in one’s imperfections. MILEY CYRUS: What is it that makes you fall in love with a character? ANYA TAYLOR-JOY: It feels like less of a choice, more of an instinct. My body figures it out before I do–I start sitting differently, speaking the words aloud in a new voice. I believe every character has things to teach you. MC: Does music matter to you in movies? Can a score totally make or break a film for you? ATJ: Absolutely. I LOVE film scores and soundtracks. I make my own playlists for jobs but the few times I’ve been given a theme for a character whilst shooting, it totally changes the game. MC: What was it about Lucky that made you go, “I have to do this”? ATJ: At first, the opportunity to fully produce it alongside such impressive collaborators was hugely appealing but I didn’t want to jump in unless I felt I had something to add. Luckily, reading the book I immediately saw the texture of the world and through the empathy I felt for her, I knew this was material I could sink my teeth into and expand. MC: You executive produced Lucky and Sacrifice. What made you want to get more involved from the ground up? Was it fun exercising both sides of your brain? I always think of it as the head and the heart…the boss side and the creative side. ATJ: Exactly. It honestly felt like something I had always been doing, it just now had a job title. I’ve never been able to not think of the project as a whole–I’m obsessed with how something moves, feels, sounds. It’s all storytelling. As a producer you get to help design the world your character lives in. I’m in love with all aspects of filmmaking so to have the ability to play in all the different sandboxes is a thrill.MC: When you step back into a world like Dune, how do you keep it fun for yourself? I imagine there’s so much pressure on a film that big, and I know you love to have a good time, so how do you make sure you don’t lose that? ATJ: I’ve never let that be a concern. Of course I hope fans will be happy with the end result, but I never forget that I myself am a fan. Of the world, the filmmaker, the character. I approach every job the same–with complete commitment to the present, an open heart and wild curiosity. It’s all an adventure! MC: I know travel is such a huge part of your life, and unlike me, you actually love being away from home. What’s one of your favorite places you’ve ever been? And what’s the one thing you always pack besides your hot husband? ATJ: Ooooh, I loved trekking with gorillas in Rwanda. Africa in general is extraordinary. Japan is exquisite. On Dune, I did a couple of side quests to Austria and South Korea. My blessing and my curse is I always travel with an insane amount of books. Nearly a full suitcase. Wish I could get behind a Kindle, but nothing beats holding a physical copy in your hand. MC: Dune has one of those fan bases that’s so passionate. Do you ever think about expectations? And whose opinion matters most to you? Is there someone in your life you’re still secretly trying to impress? ATJ: Oh wow. That cuts deep. I think I’m still trying to impress myself? I have absurdly high standards that can be exhausting at times. Not so much for other people but personally. I care so much about the creation that I want to make sure I’ve given it my best. Growing up has meant I’ve learned that sometimes perfection is in letting go. MC: Fame is part of the job, and it exposes parts of our lives that have nothing to do with the work. How have you learned to protect the parts of yourself that are just yours? ATJ: If anything, I think I’ve protected myself too much. It took me a minute to not feel hunted, to not want to hide. I’ve learned to take things less seriously by choosing which opinions actually matter to me and which are based on very little information at all. MC: What else outside of acting has been inspiring you lately? What are you finding yourself wanting to make outside of film? ATJ: Travel! Music. Older films. Nature. Clothessss. MC: I love that you journal. Has writing always been your way of making sense of your emotions and everything going on in your head? ATJ: Absolutely. It started first with wanting to remember my dreams. I’ve always had an active dream life–sometimes it feels more real than this one! Writing is such a sanctuary. Even if you don’t see the value in what you’re writing in the moment, with time you’ll notice little clues. Oscar Wilde wrote, “I never travel without my diary. One should always have something sensational to read on the train.” MC: What’s one of your favorite looks you’ve ever worn? Mine is obviously the Bob Mackie you wore at my Hollywood Walk of Fame ceremony. You looked so gorg. ATJ: Thanks, angel. Any time I’ve worn Bob it’s been special. I wore a butter yellow Dior Haute Couture gown to my first Emmys with a low, low back and a huge canary yellow train. That one came in a dream and to see it come to life so beautifully was magic. MC: You have such a unique look. Did you ever have an awkward phase, or a time where you felt unsure in your own skin? ATJ: Oh yes, haha. I still do! I think that’s one of the lessons of life; we spend so much time analysing and trying to force our physical bodies to comply to whatever the current beauty standard is that we forget to enjoy its very existence. Whilst it still creeps up, I’m done with that. I’m way too grateful for the wonders it allows me to experience and the beauty it helps me produce. It’s my vehicle for fun. MC: When you think about everything that’s still ahead, what genuinely excites you the most that we wouldn’t expect? ATJ: Expanding my unjaded heart. Getting sillier. Feeling everything. And stretching beyond my imagination. ATJ: Hardddd. It’s a toss-up between a snow leopard, a hummingbird, and a killer whale.
